# Part 1 — The rules that hold everywhere

Each ends with its **test**, so whether a session complied is never a matter of opinion.
**"The owner"** is Zach.

**R1 — Absolute dates only.** `2026-09-14`, never "today", "recently", "last week".
*Test:* `grep -niE 'today|yesterday|recently|last (week|month)|this (week|month)'` over what
you wrote returns nothing.

**R2 — Every claim carries a citation.** `file:line`, a filename, a commit hash, a migration
name, the query that produced it. A claim with no citation is a guess and will be treated as
one.
*Test:* every sentence stating what the code, the data or the tooling does names its source;
one that cannot is deleted before hand-off.

**R3 — A claim in an existing doc is a lead, not a fact.** Re-verify before building on it.
This applies hardest to `AGENTS.md`, `agents/rules/**` and `students.md`: they are upstream
Cal.com's, describe a fast-moving codebase, and are not maintained against this fork.
*Test:* a claim carried forward appears with `verified <date>` and the citation from your own
check, not the original's.

**R4 — Grep before recording an absence.** "Nothing does X" is the most expensive kind of
wrong claim, because everything downstream is built on it. In a monorepo this size
(`apps/`, `packages/` — 596 Prisma migrations alone) the odds that a thing exists somewhere
are much higher than they feel.
*Test:* every "nothing does X" and "there is no X" carries the grep or query that produced it.

> **Worked example — another repo.** A handoff recorded "there is no vision anywhere in the
> repo". Vision was live the whole time in a helper file. On that track, "missing feature"
> claims were three for three wrong.

**R5 — When you disprove something, record the disproof where the wrong claim lives.** With
the reason it was wrong. Silent deletion means the next session rediscovers it. Where the
wrong claim is in a tracked upstream file you are not editing (R13), record the disproof in
`HANDOFF.md` under **Known API facts and quirks**, naming the file and line it corrects.
*Test:* the wrong claim is still findable, marked wrong, dated, with the disproof beside it.

**R6 — Ask the owner where he will see it, before building, in one batch.** That is the chat,
in the same turn. Questions written into a doc for async review do not get answered.
*Test:* the questions went out in one message before any code that depends on an answer was
written; the hand-back lists any still unanswered.

**R7 — For user-facing copy, never pick silently.** Write 2–3 real variations in different
registers (plain, warm, terse) and ask which. All UI strings also go in
`packages/i18n/locales/en/common.json` via `t()` (`AGENTS.md`;
`agents/rules/quality-review-checklist.md`), so the copy decision and the translation key
land together.
*Test:* the ask shows the variants with their registers named, or cites where the copy was
settled.

**R8 — Never re-litigate a settled decision.** Check for the settled/ratified marker before
treating anything as open — in `HANDOFF.md` under **Settled**, or in a spec's `decisions.md`
(`SPEC-WORKFLOW.md`). Genuinely new evidence produces a *supersession* — stated explicitly,
dated, naming what it replaces — not a quiet reversal.
*Test:* nothing carrying a settled marker is reopened; any change to one is a dated
supersession that names what it replaces.

**R9 — Descoping is the owner's call.** If something is explicitly parked, record it and stop
raising it. If nothing has been said, a finding still blocks by default: surface the judgment
call rather than making it.
*Test:* every finding not fixed appears in the hand-back as `parked by owner <date>` or
`open`; none is dropped silently.

**R10 — Report faithfully.** "Type-check green, not seen running" and "walked the booking flow
in the browser against seed data" are different claims and must never be merged. The PR
template's "How should this be tested?" section and `CONTRIBUTING.md`'s "Mention What Was
Tested (and How)" are the repo asking for exactly this; give it the true answer.
*Test:* the hand-back says which of the two it claims, per item.

**R11 — Read the matching standard in full before writing code.** Here that means `AGENTS.md`
plus the `agents/rules/*.md` files matching what you are touching — and `CONTRIBUTING.md`.
Not optional, not conditional on task size. If you have not read them this session, read them
now.
*Test:* the session's first reads include them, and the hand-back names them.

**R12 — Stop mid-file when something contradicts a settled decision.** Do not take the call
and flag it afterwards. A build-level call that merely *implements* a settled decision is
yours to take — record it as a line in the `HANDOFF.md` step, with one line on how to reverse
it.
*Test:* the contradiction reaches the owner as a question before the next edit to that file
lands.

**R13 — The repo's own conventions outrank this file.** In this repo, in order:

> **1. `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `agents/rules/**`, `SPEC-WORKFLOW.md`, `biome.json`,
> the PR and issue templates.**
> **2. This standard, where they are silent.**
> **3. Nothing else.** Personal habit is not a standard, and neither is another repo's.

Where 1 and 2 disagree, **1 wins, 2 is wrong, and 2 gets amended.** Cite their rule rather
than restating it (8.5) — `agents/rules/data-prefer-select-over-include.md`, not a paraphrase
of it. The same rule at file scale: **match the file you are in.** A diff that is visually
distinguishable from the code around it is a defect even when every line is defensible alone.
*Test:* the posture table above holds, and a reader of the diff cannot pick out the new lines
by style alone.

**R14 — A gate goes green by fixing the finding.** Never loosen a check to pass: not a Biome
rule, not a type, not an assertion, not a threshold, not a CI config. `as any` is already
banned outright (`AGENTS.md`), and a widened type, a `.skip`, a deleted assertion or a blanket
ignore is the same move wearing different clothes. **Green means the recorded baseline or
better** — which, until Known gap 1 is closed, means you must first *establish* the baseline
rather than assert one. A genuine exception is narrow, carries its reason inline
(`@ts-expect-error -- reason`), and is named in the hand-back. If a failure is genuinely not
yours, **prove it** the way Part 6 describes, and say so.
*Test:* the diff contains no new suppression, skip, deleted assertion or relaxed config
without a reason inline and a line in the hand-back; the findings count did not rise and the
test count did not fall.

**R15 — Never use an API you have not seen exist.** Options, config keys, flags, methods, CLI
arguments: verify against the version installed *in this checkout* — `node_modules`, `yarn.lock`,
the package's own types — and cite what you read. This repo pins `yarn@4.12.0`, Biome schema
`2.3.10` (`biome.json:2`) and a large pinned dependency set; a plausible invented option is the
single most common way agent-written code reaches a reviewer broken. Prisma is the sharpest
case: run `yarn prisma generate` and read the generated types rather than assuming a field
or enum exists.
*Test:* every API introduced either already appears elsewhere in the repo or carries a
citation to where its existence was verified.

**R16 — Secrets never enter the repo, the docs, or a pasted transcript.** No credentials, no
`.env` contents, no tokens, no connection strings — not in code, not in a fixture, not in a
doc, not in a pass-off prompt, not in a log you paste. `.env` is gitignored
(`.gitignore:4,41`) and `NEXTAUTH_SECRET` / `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` are generated locally
(`students.md`); neither ever appears in a file that is written down. Where one must appear in
a record, **redact it in place and mark the redaction** (`[redacted: API key]`) rather than
deleting the turn. If one has already landed: say so immediately and rotate it.
*Test:* the diff and every block in the hand-back are read for credentials before either is
posted; every redaction is marked; any leak is named in the hand-back the same session.

# Part 2 — Where work gets written down

Two layers, and the split is the whole point.

- **The repo's layer, tracked, in the repo's format:** `specs/<feature>/` per
  `SPEC-WORKFLOW.md` — `design.md`, `implementation.md`, `decisions.md`, `prompts.md`,
  `future-work.md`, `docs/`, plus the feature's own `CLAUDE.md`. Opt-in by the repo's own
  terms ("use spec-driven development"). **This is Profile P under other names. Use it as
  written; never rename its files to this standard's vocabulary, and never reshape an
  existing spec to match this file** (R13, 0.3 of the source protocol).
- **The private layer, untracked:** `HANDOFF.md` and `PASSOFF.md` at the repo root, excluded
  per the header. This is Profile L, and it is the default for everyday work.

**Which one.** Coursework here arrives as a stream of mostly independent items and one person
decides everything, so **Profile L is the default**. Open a `specs/<slug>/` folder — in the
repo's format, committed like any other repo file — when an effort will span many sessions,
touch several packages, or need decisions ratified before code. When both exist, the ledger
step points at the spec; the spec never points back at the ledger, because nobody else can
read it.

## `HANDOFF.md` — what is true

Read first by every session. Append-only in its log; standing sections edited in place when
stale. Sections, in this order:

- **Orientation.** What this project is (a course-org fork of Cal.com at
  `CSCI-435-SE/cal.diy`), that the owner is interactive, and the read-first list:
  `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `AGENTS.md`, the matching `agents/rules/*.md`, then this file.
- **Environment.** The verified build/test/gate commands with their **recorded baselines**,
  tool versions, and the setup recipe from Part 6 — each one run before it was written.
  **State plainly what an agent cannot do here.** Currently that list includes: no
  `node_modules`, no `.env`, no `yarn`, no Docker on PATH; no ability to see a rendered page
  without a running dev server; and no ability to trigger CI, which is label-gated to
  maintainers.
- **Settled: `<topic>`** — one section per area, stating what the product *is*, dated.
  **Do not re-ask anything under Settled** (R8).
- **Code map.** Where things live, one line each, updated by the session that adds a file.
  Start from `AGENTS.md` §Project Structure and `agents/rules/reference-file-locations.md`
  rather than re-deriving it.
- **Invariants.** The rules that compile fine when broken — `select` not `include`, never
  expose `credential.key`, permission checks in `page.tsx` not `layout.tsx`, never edit
  `*.generated.ts`. Each one cites the `agents/rules` file that owns it.
- **Known API facts and quirks.** Platform behaviour learned the hard way, with citations —
  including disproofs of upstream docs (R5).
- **The step log.** Numbered, append-only: `N. **Title.** Done <date>. <what changed, why,
  what is now fixed, which decisions it answered>`. Steps are addressable forever. Two rules:
  **take the next free number by reading the file**, and **do not edit a step you did not
  write** — append a correction as a new step.

## `PASSOFF.md` — what is next

A board plus one standalone prompt per item (Part 3). The board is the parallelism model:

| # | Task | Status | Model | Lane | Waits on | Files it owns |
|---|------|--------|-------|------|----------|---------------|

- **Lanes run in parallel; items inside a lane run in order.** Each open lane is its own
  worktree under `.claude/worktrees/` (already excluded from git — verified
  `.git/info/exclude`).
- **"Files it owns"** is the collision check. Two items naming the same file do not run at the
  same time, whatever their lanes say.
- **Status** uses the vocabulary below, and `DONE` points at the ledger step that is the real
  record: `DONE — HANDOFF 24`. **Do not paste a prompt marked DONE.**
- **A prompt rots the moment it is executed.** The ledger step is the truth; the prompt is the
  ask. Where a DONE prompt turns out to describe the work wrongly, say so on the board rather
  than editing the prompt into a lie.
- **An item exists before work on it starts:** a row, plus a dated paragraph under the board
  saying why it exists and what it came out of. An item settled as *no* stays on the board
  with its reason.

**An item is ready to be picked up when:**

- its acceptance is **checkable** — "Escape dismisses the focused toast, and does nothing when
  none is focused", not "improve the toast UX";
- its claims about the current code carry `file:line`, or it makes no claims at all (R2);
- nothing on it is an open question waiting on the owner (R6);
- what it depends on has landed, or is named and sitting at `HELD`;
- **for a feature, the issue is approved** — `CONTRIBUTING.md` requires a core team member to
  remove `🚨 needs approval` before feature work starts. Bugs, security, performance and docs
  may start immediately. This is the repo's rule and it outranks the board.

When an item fails this bar, say so on the board, ask the one batched question, and take a
ready one meanwhile.

## Status vocabulary

Use these words and no others, so a board can be scanned:

`OPEN` · `IN FLIGHT` · `DONE — <ledger step>` · `HELD` · `SETTLED AS NO` · `SUPERSEDED`

For a `specs/` effort, its `implementation.md` already carries a status field
(`not-started` / `in-progress`) — use the repo's words there, and this vocabulary only on the
private board. `DONE` always points at the record. `HELD` always names what it waits on.
`SUPERSEDED` always names what replaced it. `SETTLED AS NO` always carries the reason, because
its whole job is to not be re-proposed.

## Entering in the middle

- **A defect list from a real session** (a browser pass, an owner walkthrough) skips scoping —
  the findings *are* the scope. Give it the same done-when and watch-for shape.
- **An audit** produces its findings as ground truth and then enters at scoping.
- **A resumed effort** re-verifies its facts before executing anything: days-old plans have
  stale numbers, closed findings, and upstream merges underneath them.

# Part 3 — The pass-off prompt

**The single highest-leverage artifact in this standard.** Every session ends by writing the
next one's first message. It must stand alone: the next agent will not see this conversation.

Nine parts, in this order. Skip one only when it is genuinely empty, and say so. A prompt gets
pasted and pinned, so R16 applies to it like any other artifact.

**1 — Title.** Imperative, naming the change, not the area.

**2 — The header line.** `**Model: <tier>. Lane <X>. Waits on <what>.**` Plus the worktree
instruction when the item needs its own (Part 6).

**3 — Orientation.** Who you are picking up, what to read first and in what order, and the
session rules restated *inline* — not by reference. Repeating them in every prompt is
deliberate: a prompt is pasted alone, and a rule one file away is a rule that does not arrive.

**4 — Why this exists.** The product reason, in product terms.

**5 — What is fixed.** *"Read these before changing anything; do not relitigate them."* The
verified facts with citations: which files hold what, the invariants, the house precedent to
copy rather than reinvent (R13), the constraint that makes this smaller than it looks. This
section is where a session's reading is *banked* instead of re-paid.

**6 — Do these, in order.** Numbered steps, each carrying its reason and its constraint.

**7 — Ask before building.** The named decisions that are the owner's, each with what makes it
a real question. Explicitly: *the answer may be no.*

**8 — Not in scope, whoever asks.** The negative list, named.

**9 — Hand back.** Exactly what must be green (the literal commands, against the recorded
baseline), what the owner should do and see, and the two commit blocks Part 11 specifies.

### Template

```
## <N>. <Imperative title>

**Model: <tier>. Lane <X>. Waits on <nothing | item N | issue approval>.**
<Worktree instruction if this item needs one.>

You are picking up cal.diy (CSCI-435-SE fork of Cal.com). Read HANDOFF.md first — the
setup recipe, the gate commands, the baselines, the invariants and the code map are
there; do not re-derive them — then CONTRIBUTING.md and AGENTS.md, then the
agents/rules/*.md files matching what you are touching. Session rules: <the 2–3 that
matter, inline>.

**Why this exists.** <product reason>

**What is fixed.** Read these before changing anything; do not relitigate them.
- <verified fact with file:line>
- <invariant, and what breaks if it is broken>
- <the house precedent to follow rather than invent, cited to agents/rules/...>

Do these, in order:
1. **<step>.** <why, and the constraint it must respect>
2. …
<N>. **Record it.** <the HANDOFF step this session owes, and what goes in it>

Ask before building: <the owner's calls>.
Not in scope, whoever asks: <the negative list>.

Hand back: <the exact gates, green, at or above the recorded baseline>; <what the owner
should do and see>; the two commit blocks (git add of exactly these files, then git
commit) — do not run them.
```

---

# Part 4 — Model selection

## The driver — the model the session runs on

**The discriminator is: can the failure be silent?** Not how big or scary the work feels.
Sizing by fear over-assigns the expensive tier.

| Driver | Model | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| **Deep** | Fable 5.1 (`claude-fable-5-1`) | Only where a mistake compiles, passes every gate, and is wrong in production: payment and refund paths, booking/slot correctness, round-robin and lucky-user selection, calendar sync and merge rules, a notification or webhook that must never double-send, anything touching `credential.key`. Prefer **one narrow Deep review of a short load-bearing path** over a whole Deep phase — and that review can be a subagent. |
| **Default** | Opus 5 (`claude-opus-5`) | The default and the right answer for most work. Anything where failure is loud — a build break, a red gate, a wrong screen. Also fully-specified Prisma migrations: high stakes, low reasoning. |
| **Mechanical** | Sonnet 5 (`claude-sonnet-5`) | Whole phases only when genuinely mechanical: close-out sweeps, a bounded rename, i18n key additions, doc reconciliation. Escalate to Default the moment a gate fails for a non-obvious reason. |

*Tier→model mapping inferred from `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`'s description of the `PASSOFF.md`
convention, not from anything in this repo — see Known gap 4.*

Every board item states its driver, and the close-out repeats it (Part 7, Block C) so the
model can be set before the next session opens. **`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` binds here: if an item
names a model and this session is not it, delegate to a subagent with `model` set, or stop and
hand off. Never do the work on the wrong model.**

## Subagents

**A context-budget instrument first, a parallelism one second.** An inventory sweep run inline
costs the lead 30–50k in file reads; the same sweep in a subagent costs it a 2k summary. In a
monorepo this size that is the difference between a phase that lands and one that compacts.

| Subagent | Use for |
|---|---|
| **Mechanical** | Inventory and mapping sweeps, call-site enumeration across `apps/` + `packages/`, grep-and-report, fixture regeneration, i18n key sweeps, doc-referrer greps — anything whose whole verification is reading the output. |
| **Default** | Design judgment, tricky debugging, review of ordinary code — anything where a wrong answer would be believed and the gates would not catch it. |
| **Deep** | One job only: a narrow adversarial review of a single short load-bearing artifact, where the whole output is the verdict. Never for sweeps, never for building. |

**Why the Deep row is that narrow.** A subagent boundary keeps only the final text, so a Deep
subagent asked to *do* work throws away exactly what the tier is for. A review is the one job
whose entire value *is* the final text.

Three rules from getting this wrong:

- **Hand it your hypothesis, not a blank question.** *"Where does the dismiss logic live?"*
  invites a confident invention. *"I believe it lives at `X:88` and the only caller is `Y:41` —
  what am I missing, and is there an existing registry I should use instead?"* can be **wrong
  in a way you will notice**. This holds for your own first read of an unfamiliar area too:
  locate it yourself, then use the agent to confirm or disprove.
- **A subagent spawned into the shared worktree will edit source even when asked only to
  review.** Give anything analytical its own worktree, and check the diffstat when it returns.
- **Never let a subagent inherit the session's tier for read-and-report work.** Pass the model
  explicitly, every time.

---

# Part 5 — Context budget

## Ceilings

A phase is sized to its driver's ceiling. **This is the primary division criterion, ahead of
conceptual tidiness.**

| Driver | Ceiling | Start landing at |
|---|---|---|
| **Mechanical** | ~500k | ~400k |
| **Default** | ~400k | ~300k |
| **Deep** | ~250k | ~150k |

*A ceiling is the context size at which a tier's sessions were observed to start compacting.
Measured 2026-08-16 in an unrelated repo; they are a property of the model and harness, not of
the repo, so they are inherited as they stand and re-measured only when a tier's model
changes.* The consequence worth planning around: **assigning Deep also shrinks the phase.**

## The rule

**Within ~100k of the ceiling, stop expanding scope, find a stopping point, and write the next
agent's prompt.** Landing means: finish or cleanly abandon the edit in hand, run the gates on
what exists, print the commit blocks, write down exactly how far you got, and hand off *the
remainder*.

**A phase that ends cleanly at 60% of its scope, committed and documented, is worth more than
one that compacts at 100%.**

## Measuring it

**An agent has no automatic awareness of its own context size.** In the Claude Code harness it
is measurable on demand: the newest assistant message's
`input + cache_creation + cache_read` in the session transcript.

```bash
python3 - <<'PY'
import json, glob, os, re
SENTINEL = ""   # a distinctive phrase from THIS session; see the note below
proj = re.sub(r'[^A-Za-z0-9]', '-', os.getcwd())
files = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.expanduser(f'~/.claude/projects/{proj}/*.jsonl')),
               key=os.path.getmtime, reverse=True)
f = next((p for p in files if SENTINEL and SENTINEL in open(p, errors='ignore').read()), files[0])
last = None
for line in open(f, errors='ignore'):
    try: u = (json.loads(line).get('message') or {}).get('usage')
    except Exception: continue
    if u: last = u
print(os.path.basename(f),
      f"context: {last['input_tokens']+last['cache_creation_input_tokens']+last['cache_read_input_tokens']:,} tokens")
PY
```

**With parallel sessions in one repo, newest-mtime picks the wrong transcript.** Set
`SENTINEL` to a phrase unique to this conversation and it selects correctly. Note the project
key is derived from `os.getcwd()`, so **run it from the worktree you are actually in** — a
worktree under `.claude/worktrees/` has its own transcript directory.

**The transcript is an instrument, not an archive.** It is local to one machine, scoped to one
directory, and ages out. Anything that needs to outlive the session goes in `HANDOFF.md`, in
the same session, or it is gone.

Run it after the mandatory reading, and again whenever you open a new front — a second
package, the second app, a long debugging loop.

## Budget arithmetic, at planning time

- **Fixed overhead here is unusually large.** `AGENTS.md` (244 lines) plus `CONTRIBUTING.md`
  plus the relevant `agents/rules/*.md` plus this file, before a line of product code.
  Measure rather than guess: `wc -c <files> | awk '{print $1/4}'`.
- **Gate output is not free.** A failing `turbo` run across this monorepo dumps thousands of
  tokens per attempt, and the debugging loop is where budgets die. Leave headroom for three or
  four red runs — and spend the first on the baseline check in Part 6, not on a theory.

## Signals a phase is too big — split it

- It spans **two apps that ship separately** (`apps/web` and `apps/api/v2`), or web and
  atoms/embed. Each is its own phase; the second inherits the first's decisions.
- It contains **both a broad audit and an implementation.** Make the audit its own phase, or
  push it into subagents.
- It touches more than roughly **15–20 files** — which is also the repo's own PR limit
  territory (<10 code files, `CONTRIBUTING.md`), so an oversized phase is usually an
  oversized PR too.
- **It needs to read a large area to decide where to work.** That reading is a subagent's job.

The seams that keep coming out right: **schema + migration → repository → service → tRPC
router → web UI → tests and close-out.** That ordering also matches
`CONTRIBUTING.md`'s advice on how to split a large change into several PRs.

## The relay — subagent budgets

A subagent **cannot measure its own context**. So its budget is enforced two other ways.

**By construction — the lead's job.** Give every subagent a bounded, countable work-list:
*these 14 call sites*, *these 6 files*, *this one question*. An open-ended brief ("audit the
booking feature") is an unbounded one.

**By contract — put this in the subagent's prompt:**

```
Your work-list is <N> items, listed above. Work them in order.

If you reach roughly 2/3 of your budget signals — you have read more than ~25 files, or you
are past item <2N/3> with substantial work left — STOP. Do not start another item.

Instead, make your final output a pass-off prompt for a fresh agent: which items are done and
what you concluded for each, which item you stopped on and how far into it you got, the file
paths that mattered, and the exact remaining list. Write it to stand alone — the next agent
will not see this conversation.
```

**Then the lead relays.** A returned pass-off prompt is a normal result, not an error: spawn a
fresh subagent of the same model with that prompt as its brief, and repeat until the work-list
is exhausted — paying only the returned summary each time. Log each relay, so the record says
the sweep took three passes.

---

# Part 6 — Parallel sessions

The assumption throughout: **several sessions run against this repo at once, and the owner is
the only one who knows which uncommitted file belongs to whom.** Worktrees live under
`.claude/worktrees/`, which is already excluded (`.git/info/exclude`) — so a worktree never
shows up as untracked noise in the primary checkout.

## Identity and guardrails, once per machine

- **The commit identity must be one GitHub recognises.** If `user.email` is not an address
  attached to the account, commits land unattributed — no contribution history, and no fix
  short of rewriting history. For a course repo where attribution *is* part of the
  deliverable, verify it on GitHub rather than trusting the config.

```bash
git config user.name "<name>" && git config user.email "<an address GitHub knows>" && git config --get user.email
```

- **Confirm the guardrails are real before you need them.** Push a throwaway branch, confirm
  it succeeds, and confirm you **cannot** push to `main`. A rejected push there is a correct
  result, better learned now than at a hand-back.

## The fresh-checkout recipe — worktree or clone

A fresh checkout fails gates for purely environmental reasons before it fails a real one. All
of this runs on entry, **before believing any gate**:

```bash
# 0. yarn must exist. Verified 2026-09-14: neither `yarn` nor `corepack` is on PATH on this
#    machine (node is v26.7.0 at /opt/homebrew/bin/node). One of:
#       npm i -g corepack && corepack enable        # then yarn resolves from packageManager
#       npm i -g yarn@4.12.0                        # packageManager pins yarn@4.12.0
yarn --version                 # must print 4.12.0 (package.json "packageManager")

# 1. Dependencies IN THIS CHECKOUT. `git worktree add` copies none of them.
yarn

# 2. Gitignored-but-required env. `.gitignore:4,41` hides these; nothing creates them.
cp .env.example .env
#    then set NEXTAUTH_SECRET  (openssl rand -base64 32)
#         and CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY (openssl rand -base64 24)   — students.md
#    Never paste either value into a doc, a prompt or a transcript (R16).

# 3. Generated Prisma client + types. `.gitignore:69-74` hides them; missing enum/type errors
#    are this, not your code (agents/rules/ci-type-check-first.md).
yarn prisma generate

# 4. Prove it, do not assert it. Paste the output, not the word "done".
yarn type-check:ci --force
```

The three classes that bite, and all three are live here:

- **Gitignored-but-required files** — `.env` and the generated Prisma client. Without them,
  gates fail naming code you never touched.
- **Dependencies not installed in the checkout** — until they are, an intra-repo
  `@calcom/*` workspace package may resolve elsewhere, so a green typecheck proves nothing
  about your edits.
- **Caches shared across checkouts** — `.turbo` is per-checkout, but `turbo run type-check:ci`
  will happily replay a cached result. `--force` is the answer and is not optional.

  > **Worked example — another repo.** A red lint gate reporting 20 findings came back *clean*
  > when re-run with an isolated cache — the findings belonged to a sibling worktree. Re-run
  > with a fresh cache before believing a red.

**Always go through the repo's own scripts** (`yarn type-check:ci`, `yarn lint`, `yarn test`),
never a bare `tsc`, `biome` or `vitest`. The scripts route through `turbo` with the repo's
filters and configs; a bare invocation selects a different configuration and fails in ways
that have nothing to do with your change.

## Before you debug a red gate, find out whose it is

**Check whether it is red without your change**, before forming a single theory. Not by
stashing — the stash stack is shared with every other worktree and another session may pop
yours — but in a throwaway checkout of the base commit:

```bash
git worktree add /tmp/base $(git merge-base HEAD main) && cd /tmp/base && yarn && yarn prisma generate && yarn type-check:ci --force
```

A failure that reproduces there is a note in the hand-back and an item on the board, not an
afternoon. **This is also how R14's "prove it is not yours" is satisfied**: state the command,
where you ran it, and its output.

## Committing under a shared index

These bind whoever commits — which per Part 11 is the owner, running the blocks this session
prints. They are stated here because the blocks must be *correct* when printed.

```bash
git add -N <new-path> && git commit -o <path> <path> -m "..."
```

- **`git add -N` first for any file git has never seen.** `--only` silently drops untracked
  paths, and the commit still typechecks, because the files are on disk.
- **Never `git add -A`, never `git add .`**, not even scoped to a directory. It sweeps up
  another session's in-flight work — and it is the one command that would drag this
  standard's own files toward a commit. Git refuses an explicitly named excluded path; that
  refusal is the net working and is **never** answered with `-f`.
- **Commit early, in small slices** — after each leg lands, not once at the end. This is also
  the repo's own rule (`CONTRIBUTING.md`: <500 lines, <10 code files).

  > **Worked example — another repo.** A whole feature build was swept into a parallel
  > session's commit while its author was still running gates.

- **Never `git checkout --` or bare `git stash`/`git stash pop` to undo an experiment.** Both
  reach files that are not yours, and the stash stack is shared across every worktree of this
  clone. Copy the file aside and restore it with `cp`, or make a throwaway WIP commit.
- **After a split commit, build HEAD in isolation before pushing.** Gates run against the
  working tree, not HEAD, so a partial commit can leave the branch unbuildable while your tree
  is green:

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/headcheck && git archive HEAD | tar -x -C /tmp/headcheck && cd /tmp/headcheck && yarn && yarn prisma generate && yarn type-check:ci --force
```

- **Shell working directory resets between calls in some harnesses.** Use absolute paths for
  anything whose answer depends on which checkout you are in.

## Numbered shared resources — Prisma migrations

`packages/prisma/migrations/` holds **595 migrations plus `migration_lock.toml`** (verified
2026-09-14), named `YYYYMMDDHHMMSS_description`. They are timestamps, not a sequence, so two
sessions do not collide on a *number* — they collide on **order**, which is worse because it
is silent: a migration with an earlier timestamp created later will be applied out of the
order it was written against.

- **Derive the timestamp at the moment you create the migration**, from the clock, via
  `yarn prisma migrate dev --create-only --name <name>` (`agents/rules/data-prisma-feature-flags.md`).
  Never copy a timestamp from a doc, a plan or this file.
- **Read names, not counts.** `ls | wc -l` is not the latest migration.
- **Rebase onto `main` before pushing a migration**, and re-check that yours is still last.
- `check-prisma-migrations` only runs in CI when `schema.prisma` or `migrations/**` changed —
  so it will catch drift in your PR, and nowhere else.
- Schema changes are on `AGENTS.md`'s **Ask first** list. They are the owner's call.

## Other shared state

- **A dev server already listening on the port** will be reused, which then silently tests the
  previous build. Kill any hand-started one first.
- **A test database pointed at the wrong target** can skip every test and still print `ok`.
  Grep the output for skips rather than trusting the exit code, and check the count against
  the recorded baseline. `agents/rules/ci-check-failures.md` also names two CI-only errors to
  ignore outright ("password authentication failed for user postgres", "Invalid URL").
- **A warm client reading cache** can make a data fix look unfixed. If the server log shows no
  request, you are reading cache, not the system.

# Part 7 — Closing a piece of work

**Every item ends the same way, in this order, without being asked.** The point is that the
owner can close the session immediately after: set the stated model, paste the blocks, go.

### 1 — Read your own diff, top to bottom

Before the record, before the blocks. `git diff` and `git status --short`, every hunk, looking
for the things that pass gates and fail people:

- **a credential, token or `.env` line anywhere in it** (R16) — checked first, because it is
  the only item here that cannot be fixed after the fact;
- an API, option, Prisma field or enum you did not verify exists in this checkout (R15);
- `include` where `select` belongs, or any query that could return `credential.key`
  (`agents/rules/data-prefer-select-over-include.md`; `AGENTS.md`);
- `as any`, anywhere (`AGENTS.md`);
- a test that asserts the mock rather than the behaviour — green, worthless, and it will be
  trusted;
- anything loosened to go green: a widened type, a disabled rule, a `.skip`, a deleted
  assertion (R14);
- comments describing *what* the line does, and any protected comment deleted (Part 11;
  `agents/rules/quality-code-comments.md`);
- **files touched that the task never named** — the scope creep is the finding;
- a barrel import, or an import that does not match the file it lives in (R13).

Anything you cannot explain does not ship. Delete it or understand it.

### 2 — Update the record

- One new `HANDOFF.md` step at the next free number (read it; do not trust one written
  elsewhere), naming what changed, why, what is now fixed, and which questions it answered.
  Add new files to the code map. Do not edit a step you did not write.
- For a `specs/` effort, also update that spec's `implementation.md` and `decisions.md` **in
  the repo's own format** (`SPEC-WORKFLOW.md`) — those are tracked and go in the commit.
- **The `HANDOFF.md` record is updated in the same session and never appears in a commit.**
  The commit carries the code (and any `specs/` update) alone, its message in the repo's own
  style — conventional commits, `feat:` / `fix:` / `refactor:` (`AGENTS.md`) — with no
  reference to a ledger step nobody else can read.
- **Landed early on budget, or interrupted?** Same ritual, different header: leave the item
  unmarked, add a status note — what is done, what is left, what it changes about the plan —
  and write the handoff. The pass-off then targets *the remainder of this item*. Also write a
  handoff when work crosses a model boundary. If the owner says stop, stop; mid-item is fine.

### 3 — Post three blocks in the hand-back

In the chat, not only in the docs: the whole value is that they are copy-pasteable at the
moment the session ends.

- **Block A — the pass-off prompt.** Part 3, in full, as a fenced block. It must stand alone.
- **Block B — the runtime entries this piece added.** The lines the owner walks, pasted here
  while the work is fresh.
- **Block C — the next session's model, on its own line.** `Next session: <tier>` — plus one
  clause on why, if it differs from the last. Last in the message, because it is the first
  thing the owner acts on.

Then the two commit blocks from Part 11, which the owner runs.

### 4 — State plainly what was and was not verified

R10. Give the gate counts against the recorded baseline rather than the word "green"; name any
exception taken under R14; name any pre-existing failure you are claiming is not yours, with
its evidence from Part 6; name any redaction made under R16. If a gate could not be run at
all — which, until Known gap 1 is closed, is the normal case — **say that, rather than
reporting the ones you could run as if they were the set.**

## Recording what actually shipped

**Every deviation from the plan is written back under the decision it deviates from** — not as
a changelog at the bottom, not in a commit message, but inline where someone reading that
decision will hit it. This is the anti-drift mechanism, and the single habit that separates
documentation you can trust from documentation you cannot.

Record equally: when the plan left a choice open and the build picked one; when the build found
the plan's premise wrong; and when a scope item was dropped. Refresh the live numbers too — the
gate baselines if they legitimately moved, the latest migration name, any dial that got a real
value.

## The runtime pass

**Each piece of work writes its own runtime entries as it goes**, and pastes them into the
hand-back at close (Block B). Not reconstructed later. An entry is three lines:

- **Goal it is checking** — what behaviour should now be true, in product terms.
- **Where** — the exact screen or endpoint, and how to reach it (which is also what
  `CONTRIBUTING.md` asks the PR description for).
- **What the right answer is** — including the fixture. If the check needs specific data, give
  the query or the seeded user that finds it (`yarn db-seed` creates `free:free` and `pro:pro`
  — `agents/rules/reference-local-dev.md`), not an id that will rot.

The owner walks the pass. **It does not block the work or the close-out.** What it blocks is
*claiming* something was seen working when it was not. Findings fold back as a new item, not
as ad-hoc fixes.

## Archiving a `specs/` effort

`SPEC-WORKFLOW.md` does not define an archive step, and inventing one for a tracked directory
would be setting policy in someone else's repo (R13). So: **leave a closed `specs/<slug>/`
where it is**, mark its `implementation.md` status as complete in the repo's own words, and
record the closure — plus anything the spec leaves behind that still governs the code — in
`HANDOFF.md` under **Invariants** or **Known API facts**. A rule nobody can find is a rule
nobody follows.

`docs/agent/archive/` exists for the *private* layer only: a superseded ledger, an old board.
Before moving anything there, grep for referrers — `git ls-files | xargs grep -l <filename>` —
and verify each file actually arrived before trusting the deletion.

**This standard applies forward from 2026-09-14.** Work done before then is a historical
record, not a conversion target. Do not retrofit.

# Part 8 — Doc craft

## 8.1 The code standard

**This repo already has one, and it is not this file.** `AGENTS.md` plus the 33 files in
`agents/rules/`, organized by the section prefixes in `agents/rules/_sections.md`
(`architecture-`, `quality-`, `data-`, `api-`, `performance-`, `testing-`, `patterns-`,
`culture-`, `ci-`, `reference-`), each with an impact level. **Cite those files by path; never
restate their content here** (R13, 8.5). If a rule is missing from them, the correct move is a
PR against `agents/rules/` on the repo's own terms — not a private rule that only your agent
obeys.

Two things this standard adds that they do not cover, and that belong in any rule you *do*
propose upstream:

- **An enforcement tag.** *lint* (Biome catches it) · *gate* (`type-check:ci` or a test catches
  it) · *CI* (a job catches it — **and say which label the job needs**, given the gating
  above) · *review* (nothing catches it). The tag tells a reader whether a clean run means
  anything. Most `agents/rules/` entries are *review*-class, which is exactly why they are
  worth reading.
- **A provenance label where a rule is a choice:** *[STANDARD]* canonical for the ecosystem ·
  *[COMMON]* widespread, alternatives named · *[OURS]* a house preference. This is what stops
  a later agent "correcting" a deliberate call.

**Where Biome settles something, the config is the rule and prose says nothing.** `biome.json`
fixes line width (110), indentation, line endings and import grouping. A short standard for a
language with strong tooling is not missing rules; it is correctly scoped.

**Sanctioned divergence.** API v1 and v2 diverge on purpose, and
`agents/rules/api-no-breaking-changes.md` owns the rule: a changed behaviour is a *new
versioned endpoint*, and the old one keeps working. Anything else that differs between
`apps/api/v1` and `apps/api/v2`, or between `apps/web` and `packages/platform/atoms`, is drift
until someone writes down why it is not.

## 8.2 The docs index

The repo has no docs index (`docs/` holds `api-reference/v2/openapi.json` and five empty
sprint folders — verified `git ls-files docs`). Do not create one for it unilaterally.

The **private** layer's index is `HANDOFF.md` itself: its code map and its step log are what
make anything findable. Every private doc gets a line there — what it is, whether it is
current, and the date last verified.

## 8.3 Standing rules that outlived their doc

A section in `HANDOFF.md` for rules that are still true of the code after the effort that
produced them closed. Each is one paragraph: the rule, why it exists, and the spec or step it
came from.

## 8.4 Prose rules for all of it

- R1, R2 and R5 apply to every sentence in every doc: absolute dates, citations, disproofs
  recorded in place. Docs are append-and-amend, not rewrite.
- State what is true, flatly. Reserve "should" for things that are not yet true.
- Write the counter-argument down next to the decision it lost to. Unrecorded, it returns in
  three weeks as a new objection.

## 8.5 Vendored authority — mirrors

Where a rule that binds this work lives **outside** the repo — upstream Cal.com documentation,
an API contract, a vendor spec — vendor a copy rather than paraphrasing it, and cite the copy:

```
docs/agent/reference/<name>.md   # header: fetched <absolute date>, canonical <url>
```

Three rules make a mirror worth having:

- **Cite, do not restate.** A paraphrase drifts from its source silently and nobody can see
  that it has. "per `docs/agent/reference/upstream.md` §4" cannot drift; it can only go stale,
  visibly, against a date.
- **Never edit a mirror to agree with your docs.** If they disagree, your docs are wrong
  (R13). Fix yours, and record the disproof where the wrong claim lived (R5).
- **Every mirror carries the date it was fetched and the canonical location**, and the
  canonical one always wins.

This applies to `agents/rules/**` in spirit but not in mechanism: those are already *in* the
tree, so cite them by path directly. Never copy their text into a private file.

---

# Part 9 — The router

The file every session receives whether it asks or not. **This repo's `CLAUDE.md` is a symlink
to the tracked `AGENTS.md` — editing either edits the repo's own policy, which is not yours to
set (R13).** So the router lives in **`CLAUDE.local.md`** at the repo root, excluded from git
per the header, carrying only what is personal. See Known gap 3: whether this harness loads
that file is unverified. If it does not, move this content into `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` as a
conditional stanza — *"in any repo containing `docs/AGENT-PRACTICES.md`, read that first"* —
which applies everywhere and is never committed anywhere.

**Two layers.** `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` carries what is true of *you* across every repo — the
commit policy, the model-assignment rule. `CLAUDE.local.md` carries what is true of *this
checkout* and is personal. `AGENTS.md` carries what is true of the *codebase* and belongs to
the repo. Do not duplicate between them, and never move a personal preference into the tracked
file: the harness loads `AGENTS.md` for every contributor, so a line in it imposes your
workflow on everyone else's agent.

Keep the router short enough that its cost is worth paying on every session. Its Commands
section points at `HANDOFF.md`'s Environment section rather than repeating it.

---

# Part 10 — Agent memory

Where the harness offers persistent memory, it holds **one fact per file**, indexed by a single
`MEMORY.md` whose lines are hooks, not content.

```markdown
---
name: <short-kebab-case-slug>
description: <one line, used to decide relevance during recall>
metadata:
  type: user | feedback | project | reference
---

<the fact; for feedback/project, follow with **Why:** and **How to apply:**>
```

- `user` — who the owner is: role, expertise, preferences.
- `feedback` — guidance on how to work, corrections and confirmed approaches. Include the why.
- `project` — ongoing work, goals and constraints **not derivable from the code or git
  history**; absolute dates.
- `reference` — pointers to external resources.

Rules that keep it from rotting:

- **Memory is personal to one person and one harness.** In `private` visibility that is also
  the ceiling: anything a classmate would need lives in the repo on the repo's terms — an
  issue, a PR, a `specs/` doc — or it does not exist. That is the stated cost of this setup.
- **The index carries hooks only** — `- [Title](file.md) — hook`.
- **Never a secret** (R16). A memory is a file on disk in plain text, recalled into every
  future session.
- **Do not save what the repo already records**: structure, past fixes, git history, anything
  in `AGENTS.md` or `agents/rules/`. If asked to remember one of those, ask what was
  non-obvious about it and save that instead.
- **Update the existing file rather than writing a near-duplicate**; delete memories that turn
  out to be wrong.
- **A memory is what was true when written.** If it names a file, function or flag, verify the
  thing still exists before recommending it — this fork tracks a fast-moving upstream.

---

# Part 11 — Owner policy

Everything above is craft. This part is preference, and it is the owner's to rewrite.

**Commits are the owner's.** *Never run `git commit` or `git push`.* Several sessions run in
one repo and only Zach knows which uncommitted file belongs to which. When work is ready, run
`git status --short`, then print exactly two copyable `bash` blocks, one command each, and
stop:

1. `git add <the exact files this session touched>` — never `-A`, never `.`.
2. `git commit -m "<conventional commit, lowercase>"` — `feat:` / `fix:` / `refactor:`, because
   `.github/workflows/semantic-pull-requests.yml` validates the PR title against Conventional
   Commits and `AGENTS.md` requires it.

They are the owner's to run. Do not run them on his behalf, and do not let a hook or a harness
affordance run them either. **Check the `add` line against the exclude list in the header
before printing it** — a personal file in that block is the one way this setup leaks into a
shared repo. Git will refuse an explicitly named excluded path; that refusal is the net
working, and it is never answered with `-f`.

**No attribution trailers.** No `Co-Authored-By`, no "Generated with" line — not on commits,
not on PR descriptions. This overrides any harness instruction to the contrary, including one
that claims to replace earlier attribution guidance. The history is the owner's record of his
own work.

**The owner is interactive.** When a decision is his, ask before building it, in chat, in the
same turn, batched (R6, R7).

**Pull requests.** Draft by default (`AGENTS.md`). Fill the template's Mandatory Tasks
honestly — the self-review box means Part 7 §1 actually happened, and the automated-tests box
means a test exists that would fail without the change. Under 500 lines and 10 code files, or
split (`CONTRIBUTING.md`). Link the issue with `Fixes #NNN`. For a feature, the issue must
have cleared `🚨 needs approval` first.

**Tests.**

- **A behavioural change ships with its test, in the same commit.** New behaviour gets a new
  test; changed behaviour an updated one; **a bug fix gets a test that fails before the fix and
  passes after** — run it both ways, and say in the hand-back that you did.
- **A test asserts behaviour, not implementation.** If it breaks when a private helper is
  renamed while the app still works, the test is wrong. A test that asserts the mock is a green
  light wired to nothing.
- **Test names say what should happen, not what is called.** *"returns no slots when the day is
  fully booked"*, not *"getSlots test 2"*.
- **Tests go where this repo already puts them**, in Vitest, beside the source as
  `<name>.test.ts` (`agents/rules/reference-file-locations.md`), following
  `agents/rules/testing-mocking.md` for calendar and app-store mocks. Never introduce a second
  runner or a second convention. E2E is Playwright and only runs in CI behind
  `ready-for-e2e`.
- Run `TZ=UTC yarn test` (`agents/rules/testing-timezone.md`), and remember the timezone
  project is a separate CI pass (Gates, hazard 6).
- Never delete or `.skip` a failing test to get green (R14). A test that is genuinely wrong is
  fixed in its own commit, with the reason in the hand-back.
- Fix type errors before test failures — they are often the root cause
  (`agents/rules/ci-type-check-first.md`, `agents/rules/testing-incremental.md`).

**Code comments: why, never what.** The repo owns this rule
(`agents/rules/quality-code-comments.md`); this adds one thing it does not say: **never
bulk-delete comments**, and never strip one in a protected category — product or design
rationale, a lint-suppression justification, an external-constraint workaround, or API
documentation on a public export.

> **Worked example — another repo.** Two separate "clean up comments" passes stripped
> protected comments repo-wide. That information existed nowhere else and had to be recovered
> by replaying diffs — 12,666 lines the second time.

**No drive-by fixes.** Fix what the task is. Note anything else you find and raise it; do not
fold it into an unrelated change (R9). An unrelated change hides in the diff, and in its
review — and here it also pushes the PR past the repo's size limit.

**Helpers get extracted; functions stay short.** Roughly 6–15 lines is the house shape.

**Design tokens, never literals.** Tailwind role-named tokens, never raw hex or arbitrary
values. Follow the surrounding component (R13).

# Appendix B — What this adaptation produced

All of it untracked and excluded — `.git/info/exclude` (this clone, all worktrees) and
`~/.config/git/ignore` (every clone on this machine):

```
docs/AGENT-PRACTICES.md       this file
CLAUDE.local.md               the router (Part 9)
HANDOFF.md                    the ledger (Part 2)
PASSOFF.md                    the board (Part 2)
docs/agent/reference/         vendored authority (8.5)

- **Never `git commit` or `git push`.** Print two bash blocks — `git add <exact files>` then
  `git commit -m "<conventional, lowercase>"` — and stop. Never `git add -A`, never `git add .`
  (other sessions run in this repo). No `Co-Authored-By`, no "Generated with" line, ever.
- **`select`, never `include`, in every Prisma query**, and `credential.key` never leaves a
  query, a tRPC response or an API payload.
- **No `as any`.** Fix the type.
- **`yarn type-check:ci --force`** — without `--force` turbo replays a cached green.
- **Run `yarn prisma generate` first.** Missing enum/type errors are almost always this, not
  your code.

  "nothing does X" is usually wrong.

Yarn 4.12.0 / Turbo monorepo · TypeScript strict · Next.js 14 (App Router in parts) ·
PostgreSQL + Prisma · tRPC · NextAuth · Tailwind · Biome · Vitest (unit) + Playwright (e2e) ·
next-i18next.

## Architecture — do not violate

- Layering is acyclic: `packages/lib` → `packages/app-store` → `packages/features` →
  `packages/trpc` → `apps/web`. Never import upward
  (`agents/rules/architecture-circular-dependencies.md`).
- All DB access goes through Repository classes; no business logic in them; no Prisma outside
  them (`agents/rules/data-repository-pattern.md`).
- `packages/features/**` must not import `@calcom/trpc`. tRPC hooks live in
  `apps/web/modules/**` (`agents/rules/architecture-features-modules.md`).
- `apps/api/v2` imports `@calcom/features`/`@calcom/trpc` only by re-export through
  `packages/platform/libraries` (`@calcom/platform-libraries`).
- Permission checks in `page.tsx`, never `layout.tsx`.
- Never edit `*.generated.ts` — regenerate via app-store-cli.
- Public API endpoints never break; a changed behaviour is a new version
  (`agents/rules/api-no-breaking-changes.md`).

## Directory map

| Path | Belongs here | Does not |
|---|---|---|
| `apps/web/` | Next.js app, routes, views, tRPC hooks | framework-agnostic services |
| `apps/api/v2/` | NestJS API v2 controllers/services | direct `@calcom/features` imports |
| `packages/features/` | repositories, services, feature UI, DI modules | `@calcom/trpc` imports |
| `packages/trpc/` | routers and handlers | anything from `apps/web` |
| `packages/prisma/` | `schema.prisma`, `migrations/` | business logic |
| `packages/lib/` | cross-cutting utilities | repositories, feature imports |
| `packages/ui/` | shared primitives | feature logic |
| `specs/<feature>/` | the repo's multi-session design docs (tracked) | personal notes |
| `HANDOFF.md` `PASSOFF.md` `docs/agent/` | personal ledger/board (untracked) | anything a classmate needs |

- **Without the `ready-for-e2e` label**, build, e2e, integration and setup-db are all skipped.
  Green means lint + type-check + unit + api-v2 unit + security-audit, and nothing more.
- **Without write access or a `run-ci` label**, a PR runs zero checks and `required` fails on

- `check-prisma-migrations` runs **only** when `schema.prisma` or `migrations/**` changed.

- `yarn test` does **not** run the timezone project; CI runs it separately with

- **No baseline count has been recorded yet** — see `docs/AGENT-PRACTICES.md` §Known gaps.

## Never do this

- Commit a credential, token or `.env` line — in code, a fixture, a doc, or a pasted log.
  Redact in place, marked, and rotate anything that already landed.
- Loosen, disable, skip or delete a check to make a gate green. Fix the finding. A genuine
  exception is narrow, carries `-- reason` inline, and is called out in the hand-back.
- Use an API, option or config key you have not seen in the installed version.
- Write a test that asserts a mock instead of the behaviour.
- Bulk-remove comments, or strip a protected one (rationale, suppression justification,
  workaround, public-export docs).
- Claim something was verified when it was type-checked. "Tests pass" and "I ran it and
  watched it work" are different sentences and stay different.
- Start coding a **feature** before its issue has cleared `🚨 needs approval`
  (`CONTRIBUTING.md`). Bugs, security, performance and docs may start immediately.
- Edit `CLAUDE.md` — it is a symlink to the tracked `AGENTS.md`.
- Run `git commit`, `git push`, `git add -A`, bare `git stash`, or `git checkout --`.

Consequence worth naming up front: **branch `short` has no commits.** Everything produced is excluded by design.

## Four findings from the inventory

1. **CI lies in two ways, both by design.** A Markdown/docs-only PR runs *no checks at all* and `required` still passes (`pr.yml` paths-filter). And without the `ready-for-e2e` label, every build, e2e and integration job is skipped — "green" means lint + type-check + unit + api-v2 unit + security-audit, nothing more.
2. **No gate has been run here, and none can be.** No `node_modules` in either checkout, no `.env`, and neither `yarn` nor `corepack` is on your PATH (`node` is v26.7.0 via Homebrew). ## Where things stand

| | |
|---|---|
| `~/Projects/cal.diy` (primary) | on **`short`** ✅, clean, all four standard files + `.env` present and excluded |
| `.claude/worktrees/agent-working-standard-31cd75` | back on `claude/agent-working-standard-31cd75`, no longer holds `short` |

| Primary install | queued, starts automatically the moment the worktree one exits |

Two things worth knowing about how I did that:

- **The exclude rules already covered the primary checkout.** They went into `.git/info/exclude` via `--git-common-dir`, which is shared by every worktree of this clone — so the copied files were invisible to git the instant they landed. Verified, and `git status` in primary is empty.
- **I serialised the two installs deliberately.** `postinstall` runs `husky install`, which writes `core.hooksPath` into `.git/config` — and worktrees share that file. Two installs racing on it is a plausible way to end up with a corrupt config, so the primary install waits for the worktree one to exit rather than running alongside it.

## One thing you'll want to decide

**This session stays rooted in the worktree.** For working on `short` natively, open a new Claude session in `~/Projects/cal.diy`. I'll keep driving from here until the baselines are recorded, since absolute paths work fine.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-14 21:20:21-0400)**_

Answering your question first, because it matters more than the install:

## They're not on `short`, and they can't reach `main`

`docs/AGENT-PRACTICES.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md`, `HANDOFF.md` and `PASSOFF.md` aren't on **any** branch. They're untracked and excluded, so they live in your working directory outside version control entirely. Concretely:

- **They can't go to `main`.** Nothing can commit them — `git add HANDOFF.md` is refused, and I demonstrated that earlier. They'll never appear in a commit, a PR, or a push.
- **They don't "stay on `short`" either.** Switch to `main` tomorrow and they'll still be sitting there, because git ignores them on every branch equally. The branch is simply irrelevant to them.
- **The repo's own `specs/` folders are the opposite.** Those *are* tracked. If you start a spec via `SPEC-WORKFLOW.md`, it commits and travels to `main` through a PR like any other file. That's the deliberate split: repo-shaped work goes in the repo's own format; your private process doesn't.

The real cost is the flip side: **they're in no commit, no remote, no backup.** Delete the clone and they're gone. If you'd rather they were versioned and visible to your classmates, that's GATE 0 question 1 — say so and I'll reverse the exclusions and commit them properly.

## Meanwhile: Node 26 is not viable here

`yarn prisma generate` **exited 1**:

```
Error while deleting old data in path packages/prisma/zod:
The property 'options.recursive' is no longer supported. Received true

That's the zod generator calling a Node API removed in modern Node. `students.md` verified **Node v24.x**; you're on v26.7.0 via Homebrew. Homebrew already has `node@24` installed, so the fix is available — but it means the baseline currently being measured is on a toolchain that's already failing. Stopping it and redoing on Node 24.

## No — I have none of it, and there's a signal you should see

I searched the repo. Every "how we work" document in it is upstream Cal.com's, rebranded. What exists for the course is **empty scaffolding in two places**:

```
docs/sprint0 … sprint4/     .gitkeep only
ai-logs/sprint0 … sprint4/  .gitkeep only
```

Ten directories, zero files. `.github/CODEOWNERS` is empty too. There is no syllabus, no sprint dates, no rubric, no roster, no definition of done, and no statement of what your team is building.

**The `ai-logs/` tree is the part worth your attention.** Someone set up a per-sprint place to log AI usage. If the course requires that as a deliverable, it cuts against the assumption I built this on — I set your standard to `private` precisely so nothing imposes process on your classmates, but a required AI log is the opposite: work the course expects you to *publish*. That's worth resolving before you accumulate sessions you'd have to reconstruct later. My session transcripts are local-only and age out in about a month, so they're not a reliable source to reconstruct from.

## What's worth adding, and what isn't

Pertinent — each one changes how I'd work:

- **Definition of done / sprint rubric.** This is the big one. My posture table currently records "Definition of Done: none found." If the course has one, it *outranks* my standard (R13) and rewrites the readiness bar in `PASSOFF.md`.
- **Sprint dates and which sprint is current.** Planning and the "last session before a deadline" case depend on absolute dates.
- **What goes in `docs/sprintN/` and `ai-logs/sprintN/`.**
- **Your role, who decides, and whether the course expects team process.** I cut Part 12 (team mode) on the judgment that you're one person with a private process. If the course mandates shared process, that call should be revisited rather than left as my assumption.
- **What your team owns this term** — decides whether to open `specs/` folders.
- **Any required issue/PR workflow** (user stories, a board, linking conventions).

Not worth adding: the syllabus PDF, lecture schedule, readings, attendance policy. They'd cost context on every session and change no decision I make. And leave classmates' names, emails, and grades out of anything committed.

## Where it should go

Split by who it binds:

- **Binds the team** → the repo, tracked. It's your org's repo and the sprint folders show that's the intent.
- **Just context for me** → paste it here and I'll distill it into `HANDOFF.md` under Orientation and Settled. Private, no repo pollution, and it survives session boundaries.

Honestly, the fastest path is: answer the six bullets above in a message rather than uploading documents. That's maybe ten lines, and it's the part that actually changes my behavior.

Stop — the test output just exposed something that invalidates the test baseline:

```
❯ .claude/worktrees/agent-working-standard-31cd75/apps/api/v2/.../slots.service.spec.ts
❯ .claude/worktrees/agent-working-standard-31cd75/apps/web/app/api/webhooks/.../route.test.ts
```

Vitest running in the **primary** checkout is collecting tests from **inside the worktree**, because the worktree sits at `.claude/worktrees/…` *within* the repo root. Git ignores that path; vitest doesn't — it globs the filesystem. So the suite is running against two copies of the repo at once. Whatever count it prints is wrong, and it's a textbook "gate that lies." It has to be fixed before any test baseline is worth recording — either `git worktree move` it outside `~/Projects/cal.diy`, or remove it. You've moved off it, so I'd remove it, but that's a deletion and it's your call.

## On the AI logs

That's a **committed deliverable**, and it's course convention — so it outranks my standard and becomes a posture-table row. `ai-logs/sprint<N>/zach-short/` with a link file. Two things to pin down when you check:

- **Which sprint is current** — the folders run 0–4 and I've no way to tell which is live.
- **A link to what.** Claude Code sessions here are local transcripts that age out in roughly a month; they don't come with a public URL by default. If the requirement is a shareable conversation link, that's worth confirming early rather than at submission, because the raw material won't be reconstructible later.

Say the word and I'll create the folder and a stub link file.

## On attaching info + gitignoring it — mostly no, and the distinction matters

Don't gitignore course policy. That's precisely the material that should be **committed**:

- **Binds the team** (definition of done, sprint dates, the ai-log convention, who decides) → commit it. It's your org's repo, the sprint folders show that intent, and a gitignored rule is one your teammates rediscover the hard way and nobody can cite in a review.
- **Genuinely personal** (your own notes, scratch planning) → gitignore, and that plumbing already exists — I'd just add patterns.

For what I actually need, **pasting ~10 lines here beats attaching files.** Answer the six bullets and I'll distill them into `HANDOFF.md`; files cost you effort and cost every future session context.

One caution: if `CSCI-435-SE/cal.diy` is public, don't commit your professor's syllabus or course materials into it without checking — that's their content, and a fork of an open-source project is a conspicuous place to put it.

**Gates that can lie here.** The first five were verified by reading `.github/workflows/pr.yml`
on 2026-09-14; the last four were found by running the gates.

1. **A Markdown- or docs-only change runs no checks at all, and `required` passes.** `pr.yml`

   (`pr.yml` `trust-check`), and `required` then fails deliberately. That red is not yours.
4. **`check-prisma-migrations` only runs when `schema.prisma` or `migrations/**` changed.**
   Schema drift in any other PR is invisible.
5. **`turbo run type-check:ci` is cached.** A green run can be a replayed result. `--force`
   exists for exactly this and is not optional (`AGENTS.md`).
6. **`yarn lint` is cached too — and the documented command has no `--force`.** A run on
   2026-09-14 printed `Tasks: 11 successful ... Cached: 11 cached, 11 total >>> FULL TURBO`,
   having executed nothing. Because `AGENTS.md` prescribes `--force` for type-check and says
   nothing about lint, lint is the easier of the two to fool. Use `yarn lint --force`.
7. **A nested worktree can be collected by tools that glob the filesystem.** Claude Code places
   worktrees at `.claude/worktrees/<name>/`, *inside* the repo root. Git ignores that path
   (`.git/info/exclude`); vitest does not necessarily — on 2026-09-14 a run from the primary
   checkout reported test files under `.claude/worktrees/.../apps/...`, i.e. two copies of the
   repo at once. `type-check` and `lint` are unaffected: turbo scopes them to `package.json`
   `workspaces` (`apps/*`, `packages/*`, ...), which cannot match `.claude/worktrees/**`.
   **Check `git worktree list` before trusting a test count.**
8. **`yarn test` alone does not run the timezone project.** CI runs the suite twice — plain,
   then `VITEST_MODE=timezone` (`unit-tests.yml:20,22`), selected at `vitest.workspace.ts:7`.
9. **`yarn test` without `yarn prisma generate` fails on missing enums/types**, which reads as
   a code failure and is not one (`agents/rules/ci-type-check-first.md`). On Node 26 the
   generate step itself fails, so this compounds.

---

'''
s = s[:gstart] + gnew + s[gend:]
open(p,'w').write(s)
print("known gaps + gates rewritten")

**Two Known gaps closed**, with the disproofs recorded rather than deleted:

- **Node.** Not "unverified" any more — 26.7.0 is *broken*, 22.14.0 works. `students.md` says v24, `AGENTS.md` says nothing, `engines` pins only npm and yarn. Three sources, three answers, and the code settled it. The router now opens its Commands section with the `export PATH` line, since that's the failure that costs an hour.
- **`CLAUDE.local.md` is loaded** — this session's own restart proved it by listing the file as private project instructions.

**Two new gates-that-lie**, both found by running things rather than reading them:

- **`yarn lint` replays a turbo cache and the documented command has no `--force`.** The "clean lint exit 0" I recovered from the killed job said `Cached: 11 cached, 11 total >>> FULL TURBO` — it executed nothing. `AGENTS.md` prescribes `--force` for type-check and is silent on lint, which makes lint the easier one to fool. That's why I'm re-measuring it rather than writing the 0 down.
- **A nested worktree can be collected by filesystem-globbing tools.** type-check and lint are provably safe (turbo scopes them to `package.json` `workspaces`, which can't match `.claude/worktrees/**`); vitest is what I saw pulling in a second copy.

## One thing I'm not yet certain of

I wrote hazard 7 from a real observation — test output showing files under `.claude/worktrees/.../apps/…`. But reading `vitest.workspace.ts:57`, the includes are root-relative (`apps/**`, `packages/**`), which *shouldn't* reach that path. The collection running right now is emitting only `/Users/zachshort/Projects/cal.diy/packages/…` paths so far, so it may not reproduce. The observation was real; my explanation of the mechanism may not be. I'll correct the wording once the check finishes rather than leave a confident claim I can't reproduce.

Also worth flagging for the test baseline: **there's no Postgres** (no Docker), so whatever number lands is a baseline *without a database*, and the docs say so explicitly. === is-prisma-available-check.ts ===
import { Prisma } from "./client";

export async function isPrismaAvailableCheck(): Promise<boolean> {
  try {
    const { prisma } = await import("./index");

    await prisma.$queryRaw<unknown[]>(Prisma.sql`SELECT 1`);
    await prisma.$disconnect();
    return true;
  } catch (e: unknown) {
    if (e instanceof Prisma.PrismaClientInitializationError) {
      return false;
    }
    throw e;
  }
}

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-14 21:41:04-0400)**_

Now I have the exact mechanism, and it's a genuine defect rather than just a missing dependency.

`is-prisma-available-check.ts` catches **only** `Prisma.PrismaClientInitializationError` and returns `false`; every other error is **rethrown**. A refused TCP connection to a Postgres that isn't running doesn't surface as an initialization error, so it escapes the guard, propagates to `auto-migrations.ts`'s `main().catch()`, and exits 1.

So the chain is:

1. `CONTRIBUTING.md` says run `yarn build` before pushing.
2. `yarn build` → `@calcom/prisma#build` → `ts-node auto-migrations.ts`.
3. That runs **`yarn prisma migrate deploy`** (`auto-migrations.ts:34`) against `DATABASE_URL`.
4. Its "no database, skip gracefully" guard only handles one error class, so on a machine with no Postgres the build **fails in 20s** instead of skipping.

Two implications worth separating:

- **On a machine without a database** (this one), the documented pre-push command cannot complete. That's the honest baseline, not a gap.
- **On a machine *with* one**, `yarn build` is not read-only — it applies pending migrations to whatever `DATABASE_URL` points at. Anyone pointing `.env` at a shared or staging database and running the documented build would migrate it. That belongs in the router's "Never do this" list, not buried in a ledger.

`SKIP_DB_MIGRATIONS=1 yarn build` is the supported escape hatch (`auto-migrations.ts:17`), and that's running now to get a real build number for the rest of the monorepo. I'll write both results — the documented command's failure and the flagged run — when it lands.

## The finding worth carrying forward

The build result splits in a way that matters more than the number: **the tree builds fine, but the documented command doesn't.** `CONTRIBUTING.md` tells every contributor to run `yarn build` before pushing; that runs `prisma migrate deploy` against whatever `DATABASE_URL` is set to. On a machine with no database it dies in 20s with an error that reads like a code bug. On a machine pointed at a shared one, it quietly migrates it.

I've recorded it but deliberately **not acted on it** — no edit to `CONTRIBUTING.md` or `auto-migrations.ts`. Whether this fork diverges from upstream Cal.com is a maintainer decision, and it's a course repo where that's not yours alone to make either. It's board item 4, gated on your approval before anything gets posted under your account.

Moved — and moving it surfaced a mistake of mine worth stating plainly.

## I was wrong that the repo documents no course conventions

`ai-logs/README.md` is tracked and has been since your commit `02e09b9cb3`. I missed it because I grepped for words like `syllab|rubric|roster` that the file doesn't contain, then recorded the absence as fact. That's exactly the R4 failure the standard warns about — an expensive wrong claim, because I built a Known gap and a whole set of questions to you on top of it. The correction is written into both docs where the wrong claim lived, rather than quietly deleted.

## What the README actually specifies

Your log now matches it:

```
ai-logs/sprint0/zach-short/2026-09-14_claude-code_agent-working-standard.md
```

The convention is `YYYY-MM-DD_<tool>_<short-description>.md` with `claude-code` as the tool id, plus a sibling directory of the same name for attachments. My original filename was wrong on both counts.

## Two things you should know

# Coding conventions
# Branching and commit conventions
### Branch names
`docs|feat|fix`/`name`

example: The branch that added this document is called `docs/standards-guidelines`
### Commit names
Present tense description of largest changes.
- `Add [insert big feature]`
- `Remove [insert unneeded feature]`
- `Fix [insert bug here]`

# Pull request process
Summarize your pull request at the top. Use the same prefix standard as branch names. (i.e. doc related PR would begin with `doc:`)

If your pull request addresses anything mentioned by existing issues, link those issues in your pull request description. For pull requests that are not ready to be reviewed, they must be prefixed with `WIP:` to indicate they are a work in progress, and therefore should not be reviewed for merging.
# Testing expectations
Testing the changes locally is the baseline expectation. Additionally, tests will need to be written for any new features added.
# AI tool use
If a contributor utilizes artificial intelligence to generate code, they must **review every line generated** and have at least a basic working understanding of what the code does (i.e. an answer of "I don't know" to the question "what does this AI generated function do" would be unacceptable). The contributor also accepts full responsibility of any AI generated code. An AI agent **cannot be held accountable**.

Branch names (`docs|feat|fix`/`name`), commit names, PR process, testing expectations, AI tool use — and a **Definition of Done heading with nothing under it.**

**Nothing about AI logs or links.** Its "AI tool use" section is about accountability — you must review every generated line, understand it, and own it; an agent can't be held responsible. That's a policy about *responsibility*, not about submitting logs. So the placeholder in your log stays: `docs/sprints.md` exists on no ref, and the one standards doc that does exist doesn't define the requirement.

## Three collisions worth raising on PR #7

1. **Commit style conflicts with `main`.** The doc wants present-tense `Add …` / `Fix …`. `AGENTS.md` and `CONTRIBUTING.md` — both live on `main` — require Conventional Commits (`feat:`, `fix:`). Incompatible styles; the tracked ones win today.

None of those is mine to fix — they're the team's, on their PR.
