Sprint 0 — Project Onboarding¶
Sep 1–17 · All deliverables due Sep 17, 11:59 PM · 100 points (9% of course grade)

Sprint 0 is the onboarding sprint. Its purpose is to get every team member up and running with the project, develop a shared picture of what the system does and how it is built, establish the team's working standards, and complete a small but real software engineering workflow from beginning to end. The skills and habits you establish in Sprint 0 carry through the rest of the semester, yet these can change in later sprints.

Unfamiliar with a term in these instructions?

Check the Glossary for definitions of pull requests (PRs), continuous integration (CI), sprints, agentic AI tools, and other concepts used throughout this page.

Before you begin¶
Complete these two steps before working on any deliverable. They are prerequisites: you cannot clone the repo or submit anything without them.

1. Join Zulip¶
Zulip is the course communication platform. All announcements, Q&A, and team coordination happen there.

The Zulip invite link is posted on Blackboard and in the course Zulip — do not share it publicly.

Once you join, introduce yourself in the #general stream and find your team's stream.

2. Join the GitHub organization¶
All project repositories live in the CSCI-435-SE GitHub organization. You must be a member to clone, push branches, and open PRs.

The instructor/TA will add you individually to your team's repository in the CSCI-435-SE GitHub organization. You will receive a GitHub notification when access is granted. If you have not received access by the start of Sprint 0, post in your team's Zulip stream and the TA will follow up.

Deliverables¶
D1 — Project Setup¶
Every team member must run the project locally in order to complete the changes for Sprint 0 (see D5)

What to do:

Clone your team's repository from the CSCI-435-SE GitHub organization. You have write access; no fork needed.
Follow the STUDENTS.md guide at the root of the repo to install dependencies, run the app, and verify it works. If something is not clear in this guide, consult the official project documentation (there are links to it in the guide) or ask the TA/instructor on Zulip (use your team's stream).
Run the project's test suite and confirm the baseline passes (see STUDENTS.md for the expected baseline output).
Read the project's architecture documentation and explore the codebase enough to answer these questions:
What does the system do? Who are its users? What are its main features?
What are the main components and how do they interact?
What are the major technologies, frameworks, and external services?
How is the code organized (directory structure, key packages/modules)?
How do developers typically contribute? What is the PR and code review workflow? What are the standards for issue reporting, triage, and management?
Where to find architecture documentation (per project):

Project	Architecture / developer docs
Actual Budget	actualbudget.org/docs/contributing/
Cal.diy	docs.cal.com
Chatwoot	chatwoot.com/docs/contributing
Discourse	meta.discourse.org — developer docs
Excalidraw	dev-docs/docs/codebase/ in the repo
Gitea	docs/development.md in the repo
Medusa	docs.medusajs.com/learn
Outline	docs/ARCHITECTURE.md in the repo
Provide the following evidence in your Sprint Report (see D6 below):

Screenshot(s) of the app running locally.
Screenshot(s) of the test suite passing.
Brief written answers to the questions above (included in D6).
D2 — Feature Backlog (GitHub Issues)¶
Each team member proposes at least 4 feature ideas for the project as GitHub Issues in your team's repository. More than 4 is encouraged.

Issues, not a document

The feature backlog lives in the project's GitHub issue tracker — not in a separate file. Create each proposed feature as a GitHub Issue with appropriate labels (see below). The sprint report links to these issues.

Issue composition per member (minimum 4):

2 small or medium features — concrete, well-scoped changes a single developer could complete in roughly 1-1.5 weeks. See the issues the instructor/TA will create for Sprint 0 as reference.
2 ambitious features — larger improvements or new capabilities that would take a Sprint or more. Think about what real users of this project actually want. If your team will implement them in later sprints (to be decided), they will probably need to be broken down into more manageable tasks.
There is no upper limit. If you have more ideas, open more issues. Remember that you team will have to analyze the existing backlog of issues, decompose them, prioritize them, assign them, etc. within a given sprint so that the work reasonably fits 2.5 - 3 weeks. Therefore, it is okay to have many ideas/issues in Sprint 0.

What makes a good issue: A feature is a user-visible or developer-visible change that makes the product better: a new capability, a significant improvement to an existing one, or a meaningful non-functional improvement (performance, accessibility, security). Each issue must include:

Field	Description
Title	Short, descriptive, action-oriented (e.g., "Add keyboard shortcut to dismiss notification toasts")
Summary	what the feature is, why it matters, who benefits
User story	"As a [role], I want [action] so that [outcome]" or a short scenario of what user needs to do and how the system should respond
Rough scope	Small / Medium / Large / XL — one sentence justifying the estimate
Source	Where the idea came from (project issue tracker, personal use, docs gap, community request, etc.)
Issue labels to apply (use the project's existing labels where available; create these if they don't exist):

Label	Meaning
scope: small / scope: medium / scope: large / scope: xl	Size estimate
type: feature	This is a new capability
type: improvement	Improving an existing capability
type: bug	This is a bug
Aim high on the ambitious ones

Sprint 0 is the time to think big. Some of these features will be scoped, decomposed, or merged during Sprint 1 requirements analysis; that is expected. Propose features you would actually want to use or build.

D3 — Standards & Guidelines Document¶
Each team writes an initial standards and guidelines document for how the team will work throughout the semester. This is a living document: you will refine it as you learn more, but you must commit to a first version in Sprint 0.

Step 1 — Map existing conventions. Before writing anything, read the project's own contribution files:

CONTRIBUTING.md — coding style, PR format, commit conventions, review process
AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md — AI usage policy and agent instructions (if present)
Any linter/formatter configs (.eslintrc, rubocop.yml, gofmt settings, etc.)
The existing "Definition of Done": the activities required to solve an issue (look in CONTRIBUTING.md, official documentation, PR templates, or issue tracking/triage guidelines)
Summarize what the project already requires. This becomes the baseline your standards document adopts.

Step 2 — Adopt, adapt, supplement. For each area below, either adopt the project's existing standard, note any team-specific adaptations, or fill the gap where the project is silent:

Section	What to cover
Coding conventions	Language/framework style guide; linting/formatting tools; conventions specific to this codebase
Branching and commit conventions	Branch naming (e.g., feature/, fix/); commit message format
Pull request process	PR restrictions; required reviewers; how to write a PR description; merge criteria
Testing expectations	Which types of tests to write for which changes; minimum expectations; test naming conventions
AI tool use	Which tools the team uses; what must be logged; review responsibilities for AI-generated code; how to flag AI-assisted work in PR descriptions
Definition of Done	Adopt the project's existing DoD if one exists; supplement where it is silent. At minimum: code reviewed, tests passing, CI green, documentation updated
The document must be consistent with the project's existing contribution guidelines. Where the project's guidelines are more specific, follow the project's guidelines. Where they are silent, your document fills the gap.

Submission: docs/sprint0/standards.md in the team's GitHub repository (or equivalent — see formats below).

D4 — AI Tooling Setup¶
AI tools are required in this course. Sprint 0 establishes your team's AI workflow.

What to do:

1. Review the project's AI files. Read AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, CONTRIBUTING.md (AI policy section), and any similar files in your repo. Decide as a team whether to use them as-is, adapt them, or supplement them. Document your decision in D3 (Standards doc, AI tool use section).

2. Choose your tools. Each team member should have at least one agentic AI tool set up for code-level work:

Tool	Type	Notes
Claude Code	Agentic CLI	Recommended. Course Claude Team plan available — see below.
GitHub Copilot	IDE / agentic	VS Code, JetBrains, Cursor
Cursor	Agentic IDE	Built-in agent mode
OpenAI Codex CLI	Agentic CLI	
Gemini CLI	Agentic CLI	
You may additionally use chat-based tools (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, etc.) for non-agentic tasks such as understanding code, drafting, or research.

Course Claude Team plan: The instructor will distribute seats on a Claude Team plan for the class. This gives each team member access to Claude without the free tier's rate limits. Details and instructions will be posted on Zulip and/or Blackboard. If you cannot access the Team plan, let the instructor and TA know.

Claude account and credentials

Use your own Claude account. Do not share login credentials or account access with teammates or anyone else. Sharing credentials violates the terms of service of Claude Team plan and may lead to account suspension.

3. Set up AI log capture. Full instructions are on the AI Log Instructions page. In brief:

Agentic CLI tools (Claude CLI, Gemini CLI, Codex CLI): use SpecStory — specstory run claude wraps your session automatically.
Cursor / GitHub Copilot in VS Code: install the SpecStory VS Code extension.
Web chat (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini): use the browser exporter extensions listed on the AI Log Instructions page.
Claude Desktop: not supported by SpecStory — switch to Claude Code CLI for project work or manually collect logs (see the AI Log Instructions).
Logs should be stored in ai-logs/sprint0/<your-github-username>/ in the team repo. See AI Log Instructions for naming conventions and the issue comment format.

4. Start logging from day one. Log every agentic session starting from the moment you begin Sprint 0 work. Include a summary in D6.

Submission: No separate deliverable. But we recommend running a quick test by using Claude with SpecStory: run some prompts, collect the logs, and push them to your repository. Evidence of log setup and a usage summary are included in D6 (Sprint Report).

D5 — Code Changes and Pull Requests¶
The core hands-on activity of Sprint 0 is making real changes to the codebase and going through the full contribution workflow. Every team member should open exactly 2 pull requests in Sprint 0 (i.e., they need to work on two issues).

How the work is assigned:

The instructor will post 2–3 issues in your project's issue tracker during the first week of Sprint 0. These are small, clearly scoped changes: worked examples of the contribution workflow on your specific codebase.

2–3 team members (coordinate as a team) will implement the instructor-assigned issues.
Every other team member picks 2 issues from the team's feature backlog (D2) or the project's existing issue tracker: issues at small or medium scope.
The critical rule: implement issues you did not write. Each team member works on 2 issues that were opened by someone else on the team. No two team members implement the same issue. This forces you to communicate, read each other's specifications, and treat issues as real software requirements.

Coordinate early: decide who implements which issues before anyone starts coding.

Before you write any code:

Read the issue carefully. What exactly is being asked? Ask the author on the issue if anything is unclear.
Find the relevant code yourself first, without AI. Read the directory structure, search the codebase, inspect code files, navigate code dependencies (e.g., function/method calls), etc. Take notes on what you find. This is essentially performing "Concept location" from the incremental change process covered in class.
Then confirm with AI. Once you have a hypothesis about where to make the change, ask an agentic tool to validate or extend your understanding. Let AI help you move faster, not substitute for your own reading.
This order matters: as a first experience, we want you to locate and understand code independently so that you understand the effort concept location takes and to force you to learn on your own.

How to create your branch and PR:

All team members have write access to the team repo, so you use a branch-based workflow: one branch per issue and a PR within the same repo. (See STUDENTS.md for full background on why this is the standard professional approach rather than forking.)


# One-time setup: clone the team repo (if you haven't already from D1)
git clone https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/<your-project>.git
cd <your-project>

# Before starting each issue: sync with main
git checkout main
git pull origin main

# Create a branch named for the issue (the names are examples)
git checkout -b feat/issue-17-dark-mode    # new feature
git checkout -b fix/issue-42-toast-dismiss  # bug fix

# ... after you have made your changes, run tests ...
git add <the files you changed>
git commit -m "feat: add dark mode toggle (#17)"
git push origin feat/issue-17-dark-mode
After pushing, GitHub will show a "Compare & pull request" banner at the top of the repo page: click it to open the PR form. Select main as the base branch, write your description, and submit.

main is branch-protected

Direct pushes to main are blocked. If you accidentally commit to main locally, move the work to a branch before pushing:


git checkout -b feat/issue-17-dark-mode   # creates branch from your current state
git push origin feat/issue-17-dark-mode   # push the branch
git checkout main && git reset --hard origin/main  # restore main locally
After your PR is merged, clean up:


git checkout main  # go to main
git pull origin main  # pull changes in main
git branch -d feat/issue-17-dark-mode  # delete the branch if already merged
Requirements for each PR:

The PR must be linked to a GitHub issue (reference it in the description with Closes #<number>).
The PR description must clearly explain what changed and why, in your own words.
Tests must be written or updated for any code changed.
The PR must be reviewed by at least one other team member before merging (leave a review comment, not just approval).
The PR must pass CI if CI is configured in the project. If CI is not yet configured, note this in the PR description. We don't require CI configuration for Sprint 0.
You must be able to explain every line

You may use AI tools to help write code. However, you are responsible for understanding every line in your PR. Reviewers and the instructor may ask you to explain any part of your change at any time, including after the sprint. If you cannot explain code in your own PR, you will receive points off.

Submission: All PRs in the project's GitHub repository. Links to merged (or reviewed) PRs go in D6.

D6 — Sprint Report¶
Each team submits one sprint report summarizing Sprint 0.

Accepted formats: Markdown pushed to the repository, PDF, or Word document.

If submitting to the repo: push to docs/sprint0/report.md (or report.pdf, report.docx).

Required sections:

Section	What to include
Team	Team name (choose a cool name!); member names and GitHub usernames; project name and repository link
Project overview	What the system does; key users; main components and technologies; codebase organization. Answer the questions from D1.
Feature backlog summary	How many issues were created; themes or categories; top 3–5 features the team is most interested in pursuing during the semester. Link to the issues.
Standards document summary	Key conventions adopted; any deviations from the project's existing guidelines and why. Link to standards.md.
Completed PRs	Table: PR title, issue link, author, reviewer(s), status (merged / open), brief description of the change
AI tool usage	Per team member: tools used, types of tasks, total sessions, link to ai-logs/sprint0/<username>/ folder. Notable observations about what worked or didn't.
Release	Tag name and link to the Sprint 0 release on GitHub (see D7).
Risks and challenges	Brief description of what was harder than expected; open questions; anything that could slow Sprint 1
Sprint 1 ideas	Brief ideas on the features the team intends to tackle; any setup still needed
Length: No minimum or maximum. Be specific and concrete: vague bullet-point lists are not useful evidence.

Deadline: Sep 17, 11:59 PM.

D7 — Sprint Release¶
At the end of Sprint 0, the team creates a release tag in GitHub to mark the sprint's end state.

What to do:

Ensure all Sprint 0 PRs are merged (or in a final reviewed state) before tagging.
Check the project's latest release (or most recent version tag) to find the current version number.
Create a Git tag using that version with the -csci435-s0 suffix appended — do not bump the version number. For example, if the current version is v2.17.2, tag as v2.17.2-csci435-s0. If the project has no prior releases, use v0.1.0-csci435-s0.
Write a brief release description: what was changed in the project.

git tag v<version>-csci435-s0
git push origin v<version>-csci435-s0
Then create the GitHub release from the tag on the repository's Releases page.

Submission: Link to the GitHub release in D6 (Sprint Report). The tag must be pushed by Sep 17, 11:59 PM.

D8 — Reflection Survey (Individual)¶
Each team member must complete the Sprint 0 reflection survey individually, which aims to engage the student into reflecting on the process followed in Sprint 0, including their AI usage. The link will be distributed via Blackboard and Zulip.

Deadline: Sep 17, 11:59 PM.

Grading¶
Sprint 0 is worth 100 points (9% of the course grade). Points are awarded to the team (shared grade) except for D5 individual PRs and D8 reflection survey, which are graded individually.

Deliverable	Points	Notes
D1 — Project Setup	10	Evidence: screenshots + written answers to questions about the project in sprint report
D2 — Feature Backlog	20	Quality, specificity, and ambition of GitHub issues; completeness of required fields; appropriate labels
D3 — Standards Document	10	Coverage of required sections; grounded in existing project conventions; coherent DoD
D4 — AI Tooling Setup	5	Evidence of log capture and usage summary in sprint report
D5 — Pull Requests	30	Per member: 15 pts each PR ( 2 PRs total). Criteria: code quality, test coverage, PR description, code review, CI passing (optional)
D6 — Sprint Report	10	Completeness, specificity, and quality of evidence
D7 — Sprint Release	10	Release tag created, follows project's versioning scheme, includes release description
D8 — Reflection Survey	5	Individual; required for completion
Total	100	
Extra credit

Teams whose feature backlog (D2) demonstrates exceptional depth may earn up to 5 extra credit points on D2, at the instructor's discretion.

D5 — PR grading detail (15 points per PR):

Criterion	Points
Change is correctly implemented and does not break existing tests	5
Tests are written or updated appropriately	4
PR description clearly explains what changed and why	3
Code was reviewed by a teammate (review comment evidence required)	3
Minimum bar

A team that does not get the app running (D1), does not submit a sprint report (D6), or has no merged PRs (D5) receives a 0 for Sprint 0 regardless of other deliverables.

Submission checklist¶
Push the following to your team's GitHub repository by Sep 17, 11:59 PM:

GitHub issues created for all proposed features (D2) — labeled and linked from sprint report
docs/sprint0/standards.md (or equivalent format) — standards and guidelines document (D3)
docs/sprint0/report.md (or .pdf or .docx) — sprint report (D6)
All PRs linked in the sprint report — merged or in reviewed state (D5)
AI logs committed to ai-logs/sprint0/<github-username>/ (D4)
Sprint 0 release tag pushed and GitHub release created (D7)
D8 reflection survey submitted individually by Sep 17, 11:59 PM
Lightning Talk — Sep 22 (in class)¶
Requirements will be posted separately

Each team will deliver a lightning talk on Sep 22. Detailed requirements will be posted before that date on Zulip and the course website. The lightning talk is not part of the Sprint 0 rubric; it is a separate deliverable graded independently.

````bash
# Definition of Done

An issue is Done when every box below is true. Where this list and the project's own
guidelines differ, the project's guidelines win.

**Code**
- [ ] The change does what the issue asked, and nothing unrelated rides along.
- [ ] `yarn type-check:ci --force` passes. The `--force` is required: turbo caches results and
      will replay a stale green without it.
- [ ] `yarn lint --force` passes with no new findings. `--force` for the same reason — a bare
      `yarn lint` can print `>>> FULL TURBO` having checked zero files.
- [ ] Repo conventions followed: `select` not `include` in Prisma queries, no `as any`, no
      barrel imports, `credential.key` never returned from an API or tRPC endpoint,
      permission checks in `page.tsx` not `layout.tsx` (see `AGENTS.md`).
- [ ] UI strings go through `t()` and are added to `packages/i18n/locales/en/common.json`.

**Tests**
- [ ] Tests are written or updated for the changed behaviour. A bug fix has a test that fails
      before the fix and passes after.
````

```text
=== ezh script:      150 lines ===
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"
cd "$ROOT"

# name:one-line description — single source of truth for both the menu and completion
COMMANDS=(
  "deploy:Deploy web/ to production via the Vercel CLI directly"
  "testflight:Build native/ for iOS production and auto-submit to TestFlight"
  "ota:Publish an OTA update to the native/ production channel"
  "parity:Check every web feature exists on native and back"
  "verify:Run the conventions gate (08-verify.ts)"
  "cycles:Check for import cycles across core, web, and native"
  "test:Run the vitest suite (packages/*, web, web/e2e/fixtures, native)"
  "gates:Run every CI gate, in the order CI runs them"
  "shell:Print the ~/.zshrc snippet for the ezh function + completion"
  "help:List commands"
)

cmd_deploy() {
  # Vercel's GitHub integration here only builds commits authored dan-short (see
  # docs/README.md:775) — zach-short commits push cleanly and silently never deploy.
  # Going through the CLI from web/ (already vercel-linked) sidesteps that entirely.
  cd "$ROOT/web" && vercel --prod
}

cmd_testflight() {
  # --non-interactive + --auto-submit needs no Apple login prompt once the provisioning
  # profile has the aps-environment entitlement (it does — the push-capability blocker
  # that used to break this is resolved). Submits with eas.json's submit.production
  # ascAppId, so a finished build lands in TestFlight without a separate eas submit.
  cd "$ROOT/native" && eas build --platform ios --profile production --auto-submit --non-interactive
}

cmd_ota() {
  local message="${1:-}"
  if [[ -z "$message" ]]; then
    echo "usage: ezh ota \"<message>\"" >&2
    exit 1
  fi
  # eas update prints the runtime version it published at but never checks that any
  # FINISHED build actually carries it — a native-config change silently moves the
  # fingerprint (happened via userInterfaceStyle going to "automatic"), and the update
  # ships to nobody until a new build does. Compare against
  # `eas build:list --platform ios --limit 6 --json` before trusting a publish.
  cd "$ROOT/native" && eas update --branch production --platform ios \
    --environment production --non-interactive --message "$message"
}

cmd_parity() {
  bun scripts/check-feature-parity.ts
}

cmd_verify() {
  bun scripts/codemods/08-verify.ts
}

cmd_cycles() {
  bunx madge --circular --extensions ts,tsx packages/core/src/index.ts
  bunx madge --circular --extensions ts,tsx --ts-config web/tsconfig.json web/app
  bunx madge --circular --warning --extensions ts,tsx --ts-config native/tsconfig.json native/app
  # Read this run's output, not just its exit code: a line starting with `@/` means
  # madge couldn't resolve the app's own alias and only walked a fraction of the tree
  # before printing a clean "no circular dependency found" — a false pass, not a real one.
}

cmd_test() {
  bun run test
}
```

```text
}

cmd_gates() {
  (cd "$ROOT/web" && bunx tsc --noEmit && bun run lint && bun run build)
  (cd "$ROOT/native" && bunx tsc --noEmit && bun run lint)
  for pkg in core api config icons eslint-config; do
    (cd "$ROOT/packages/$pkg" && bun run lint)
  done
  # The golangci-lint cache is shared across every checkout on the machine and keys
  # findings to wherever they were analyzed — a red here can belong to a sibling
  # worktree, not this tree. An isolated cache is the only way to trust the result.
  (cd "$ROOT/backend" \
    && go build ./... \
    && go vet ./... \
    && GOLANGCI_LINT_CACHE="$(mktemp -d)" go run ./cmd/lintgate \
    && go run ./cmd/synchelp --check \
    && go run ./cmd/sqlgate \
    && go test -race ./...)
  cmd_test
  cmd_verify
  cmd_parity
  cmd_cycles
}

cmd_help() {
  echo "usage: ezh <command>"
  echo
  for entry in "${COMMANDS[@]}"; do
    printf "  %-11s %s\n" "${entry%%:*}" "${entry#*:}"
  done
}

cmd_shell() {
  cat <<'EOF'
ezh() { "$HOME/Projects/ezhomesteading/scripts/ezh" "$@"; }

_ezh_complete() {
  local -a subcmds
  subcmds=("${(@f)$(ezh --complete)}")
  _describe 'command' subcmds
}
compdef _ezh_complete ezh
EOF
}

cmd___complete() {
  for entry in "${COMMANDS[@]}"; do
    echo "$entry"
  done
}

# Same table drives an fzf picker on bare invocation — only when it'd actually be
# interactive, so a cron job or `ezh deploy | something` never gets asked anything.
interactive_pick() {
  local lines
  lines="$(for entry in "${COMMANDS[@]}"; do
    printf "%-11s %s\n" "${entry%%:*}" "${entry#*:}"
  done)"
  echo "$lines" | fzf --prompt='ezh> ' --height='~70%' --reverse --no-info \
    --header='select a command' | awk '{print $1}'
}

if [[ $# -eq 0 && -t 0 && -t 1 ]] && command -v fzf >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  picked="$(interactive_pick || true)"
  [[ -n "$picked" ]] || exit 0
  set -- "$picked"
fi

case "${1:-help}" in
  deploy) cmd_deploy ;;
  testflight) cmd_testflight ;;
  ota) cmd_ota "${2:-}" ;;
  parity) cmd_parity ;;
  verify) cmd_verify ;;
  cycles) cmd_cycles ;;
  test) cmd_test ;;
  gates) cmd_gates ;;
  shell) cmd_shell ;;
  --complete) cmd___complete ;;
  help|*) cmd_help ;;
esac
```

```bash
P=/Users/zachshort/Projects/cal.diy; mkdir -p "$P/scripts" && cat > "$P/scripts/cal" <<'SCRIPT'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"
cd "$ROOT"

# Node 26 (the machine default) breaks `prisma generate`: the zod generator calls
# fs.rmdir(..., {recursive:true}), removed in modern Node, and the whole command exits 1.
# Every command below goes through Node 22, so no command in this script can hit that.
export PATH="/opt/homebrew/opt/node@22/bin:/opt/homebrew/opt/postgresql@14/bin:$PATH"

# name:one-line description — single source of truth for both the menu and completion
COMMANDS=(
  "dev:Run the web app at localhost:3000"
  "db:Start Postgres and make sure the calendso database exists"
  "migrate:Apply pending Prisma migrations"
  "seed:Reseed the database (test users free:free and pro:pro)"
  "reset:Drop, recreate, migrate and reseed the database"
  "studio:Open Prisma Studio to browse the database"
  "types:Type-check everything (forced — turbo caches a stale green otherwise)"
  "lint:Lint everything (forced — a bare run can report FULL TURBO having checked nothing)"
  "test:Run the unit suite, excluding any nested worktree"
  "tz:Run the timezone test project, which the plain test run skips"
  "build:Production build, without touching the database"
  "gates:Run every gate, in the order CI runs them"
  "log:Save this project's AI session transcripts into ai-logs/sprint0/"
  "psql:Open a psql shell on the calendso database"
  "shell:Print the ~/.zshrc snippet for the cal function + completion"
  "help:List commands"
)

DB_URL="postgresql://zachshort@localhost:5432/calendso"

cmd_dev() {
  cmd_db
  yarn dev
}

cmd_db() {
  # Postgres is a brew service rather than Docker here; students.md assumes Docker, which
  # is not installed on this machine. `brew services start` is idempotent.
  brew services start postgresql@14 >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
  for _ in $(seq 1 20); do nc -z localhost 5432 >/dev/null 2>&1 && break; sleep 0.5; done
  psql -p 5432 -d postgres -tAc "SELECT 1 FROM pg_database WHERE datname='calendso'" | grep -q 1 \
    || createdb -p 5432 calendso
}

cmd_migrate() {
  cmd_db
  yarn workspace @calcom/prisma db-migrate
}

cmd_seed() {
  cmd_db
  yarn db-seed
}

cmd_reset() {
  cmd_db
  dropdb -p 5432 --if-exists calendso
  createdb -p 5432 calendso
  yarn workspace @calcom/prisma db-migrate
  yarn db-seed
}

cmd_studio() {
  cmd_db
  yarn db-studio
}

cmd_types() {
  # --force is not optional: turbo replays a cached green and AGENTS.md prescribes it.
  yarn type-check:ci --force
}

cmd_lint() {
  # Same cache trap as types, but worse: AGENTS.md prescribes --force for type-check and
  # says nothing about lint, so a bare `yarn lint` prints ">>> FULL TURBO" having checked
  # zero files and looks like a pass.
  yarn lint --force
}

cmd_test() {
  # A worktree under .claude/worktrees/ lives INSIDE the repo. Git ignores it; vitest does
  # not, and collects a second copy of every test — 830 files / 208 failed / exit 1 instead
  # of 406 / 0 failed / exit 0. --exclude is additive in vitest 4, so the config's own
  # node_modules exclusion is untouched.
  TZ=UTC yarn test --exclude '**/.claude/**' "$@"
}

cmd_tz() {
  # CI runs the suite twice; the plain run skips the timezone project entirely
  # (vitest.workspace.ts:7), so a green `cal test` has not covered these.
  VITEST_MODE=timezone yarn test --exclude '**/.claude/**'
}

cmd_build() {
  # packages/prisma's build runs `prisma migrate deploy` (auto-migrations.ts:34), so a bare
  # `yarn build` MIGRATES whatever DATABASE_URL points at. Skipping that keeps a build a
  # build. Drop the flag only when you actually intend to migrate.
  SKIP_DB_MIGRATIONS=1 yarn build
}

cmd_gates() {
  yarn prisma generate
  cmd_types
  cmd_lint
  cmd_test
  cmd_tz
  cmd_build
}

cmd_log() {
  # SpecStory buckets sessions by the directory the agent ran in, so a session started in
  # .claude/worktrees/<name>/ is invisible from the repo root and looks like it never
  # happened. Sync from each directory that has sessions, not just this one.
  local out="$ROOT/ai-logs/sprint0/$(git config user.name >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo zach-short || echo zach-short)"
  mkdir -p "$out"
  specstory sync --output-dir "$out" --local-time-zone
  for wt in "$ROOT"/.claude/worktrees/*/; do
    [[ -d "$wt" ]] || continue
    (cd "$wt" && specstory sync --output-dir "$out" --local-time-zone) || true
  done
  # Transcripts go in a repo. Read them before committing: SpecStory redacts by default,
  # but "by default" is not "verified".
  echo
  echo "Now scan for secrets before committing:"
  echo "  grep -rnE 'ghp_|github_pat_|sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}|AKIA|BEGIN .*PRIVATE KEY' $out"
}

cmd_psql() {
  cmd_db
  psql "$DB_URL"
}

cmd_help() {
  echo "usage: cal <command>"
  echo
  for entry in "${COMMANDS[@]}"; do
    printf "  %-9s %s\n" "${entry%%:*}" "${entry#*:}"
  done
}

cmd_shell() {
  cat <<'EOF'
cal() {
  if [[ "$1" == "cd" ]]; then cd "$HOME/Projects/cal.diy"; else "$HOME/Projects/cal.diy/scripts/cal" "$@"; fi
}

_cal_complete() {
  local -a subcmds
  subcmds=("${(@f)$(cal --complete)}")
  _describe 'command' subcmds
}
compdef _cal_complete cal
EOF
}

cmd___complete() {
  for entry in "${COMMANDS[@]}"; do
    echo "$entry"
  done
}

# Same table drives an fzf picker on bare invocation — only when it'd actually be
# interactive, so `cal test | tee log` never gets asked anything.
interactive_pick() {
  local lines
  lines="$(for entry in "${COMMANDS[@]}"; do
    printf "%-9s %s\n" "${entry%%:*}" "${entry#*:}"
  done)"
  echo "$lines" | fzf --prompt='cal> ' --height='~70%' --reverse --no-info \
    --header='select a command' | awk '{print $1}'
}

if [[ $# -eq 0 && -t 0 && -t 1 ]] && command -v fzf >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  picked="$(interactive_pick || true)"
  [[ -n "$picked" ]] || exit 0
  set -- "$picked"
fi

case "${1:-help}" in
  dev) cmd_dev ;;
  db) cmd_db ;;
  migrate) cmd_migrate ;;
  seed) cmd_seed ;;
  reset) cmd_reset ;;
  studio) cmd_studio ;;
  types) cmd_types ;;
  lint) cmd_lint ;;
  test) shift; cmd_test "$@" ;;
  tz) cmd_tz ;;
  build) cmd_build ;;
  gates) cmd_gates ;;
  log) cmd_log ;;
  psql) cmd_psql ;;
  shell) cmd_shell ;;
  --complete) cmd___complete ;;
  help|*) cmd_help ;;
esac
SCRIPT
chmod +x "$P/scripts/cal" && echo "=== created, $(wc -l < "$P/scripts/cal") lines ===" && bash -n "$P/scripts/cal" && echo "syntax OK ✓" && "$P/scripts/cal" help
```

| `cal log` | syncs SpecStory from the repo root **and each worktree**, since sessions are bucketed by directory |
| every command | forces Node 22 onto PATH, so none of them can hit the Node 26 prisma failure |

## Verified

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Migrations | exit 0, 14s, **105 tables** |
| Seed | **41 users, 151 event types** (`free:free`, `pro:pro`) |
| Dev server | `✓ Ready in 451ms` on `:3000` |

The screenshots above are the proof that matters: the booking page renders **"Pro Example"** with its real event types (30min, 60min, Multiple duration, paid, In person meeting, Zoom Event). That name and those rows come out of Postgres, so this is a full round-trip through the database — not Next.js serving a static shell.

**The "1 Issue" badge is real but harmless**, and I'd rather name it than let you find it later: `/sw.js` 404s in dev, so the web-push service worker in `WebPushContext.tsx` fails to register. Rendering and navigation are unaffected. It's recorded in the ledger as a known non-issue so nobody chases it as a regression.

## What I had to change, and one correction

I'd told you no database was possible because Docker isn't installed. **Wrong** — Homebrew's `postgresql@14` was already installed *and running*. So D1 needed no new infrastructure. I created the `calendso` database and pointed `.env` at `postgresql://zachshort@localhost:5432/calendso` instead of the `.env.example` default (`postgres:@localhost:5450`, which assumes Docker). That deviation from `students.md` is documented in the ledger.

One consequence worth knowing: **Mailhog isn't running** — it's the other half of the Docker compose — so anything that sends mail locally has nowhere to deliver.

## `scripts/cal`

Committable (it's a repo file, not part of the private standard). Install the shell function:

```bash
~/Projects/cal.diy/scripts/cal shell >> ~/.zshrc && exec zsh
```

Then `cal` alone opens an fzf picker, `cal cd` jumps to the repo, and `cal dev`, `cal gates`, `cal reset`, `cal log` do the obvious things — each with this session's traps baked in.

```text
# AI Log Requirements Summary

## 1. Folder Path and File Naming Convention

**Folder structure:**
```
ai-logs/
  sprint0/
    <your-github-username>/
  sprint1/
    <your-github-username>/
```

**File naming pattern:** `YYYY-MM-DD_<tool>_<short-slug>.md`

**Tool identifiers:**
- `claude-code` (Claude Code CLI)
- `claude-web` (Claude.ai web)
- `claude-desktop` (Claude Desktop app)
- `cursor` (Cursor IDE or CLI)
- `gemini-cli`
- `codex-cli`
- `copilot` (GitHub Copilot VS Code)
- `chatgpt`
- `other-<name>`

## 2. Required Log Contents

Each log must include:
- "The AI model/tool used (e.g., 'Claude Sonnet 4.5 via Claude Code')"
- "The full prompt and response history for the session"
- For agentic tools: "all file edits and commands run"
- For web chat: "any files or text you pasted as context"

A log with "only your prompts (no AI responses), or that is clearly incomplete" does not meet requirements.

## 3. GitHub Issue Comment Format

Post one comment per contributor using this structure:

| # | Tool | Log | What AI helped with |
|---|---|---|---|

Include a link to the log file. If no AI was used, note "No AI used." The comment should state your role: Implementation / Code review / Testing / Other.

## 4. Claude Code and SpecStory Instructions

**Installation:**
- macOS/Linux: `brew tap specstoryai/tap && brew install specstory`
- Windows: Download from releases page, extract, add to PATH

**Usage:**
- `specstory run claude` (instead of just `claude`)
- `specstory sync` (captures sessions you forgot to wrap, or at sprint end)

At sprint end: "run `specstory sync` one final time, then copy the sprint-related files from `.specstory/history/`" into the appropriately named folder.

## 5. Attachments and Directories

"If you used files, images, screenshots, or PDFs as context in a session, save them alongside the log in a **folder with the same name** as the log file (no `.md` extension)."

Example:
```
2026-09-08_claude-web_understanding-issue-42.md
2026-09-08_claude-web_understanding-issue-42/
  architecture-screenshot.png
  relevant-code-snippet.txt
```

## 6. Missed SpecStory Capture

If you forgot to use `specstory run`: "Run `specstory sync` after any session you forgot to wrap" to convert existing CLI tool history to SpecStory's Markdown format.
```
</details></tool-use>

## One number moved, and I'd rather explain it than hide it

The test file count went **406 → 407** between the two runs, with test counts identical (4069 / 47 / 3 both times). The only thing that changed in between is that a database now exists — so one file's *collection* depends on the DB, though it contributes no tests. Both figures are now in the ledger with that note, because a future session that sees 406 on a machine without Postgres shouldn't think something broke.

This is the third baseline caveat worth carrying: the suite reports **406 without a database, 407 with one, and 830 with a nested worktree present**. Same tree, three answers. That's precisely why the standard insists a recorded baseline names the conditions it was measured under.

```bash
new = '''cmd_log() {
  # SpecStory buckets sessions by the directory the agent ran in, so a session started in
  # .claude/worktrees/<name>/ is invisible from the repo root and looks like it never
  # happened. Sync from each directory that has sessions, not just this one.
  local stage; stage="$(mktemp -d)"

  mkdir -p "$out"

  for wt in "$ROOT"/.claude/worktrees/*/; do
    [[ -d "$wt" ]] || continue
    (cd "$wt" && specstory sync --output-dir "$stage" --local-time-zone >/dev/null) || true
  done

  shopt -s nullglob
  for f in "$stage"/*.md; do
    # Claude Code fires its own internal sessions — the editor-tab namer is one — which are
    # not development work and would pad the deliverable with noise.
    if head -20 "$f" | grep -q 'You maintain a 2-3 word tag'; then
      echo "skipped (internal tab-namer): $(basename "$f")"
      continue
    fi
    # SpecStory names files <date>_<time>-<slug>.md; the course requires
    # <date>_<tool>_<slug>.md (https://csci-435-se.github.io/ai-logs/).
    local base date slug
    base="$(basename "$f" .md)"
    date="${base%%_*}"
    slug="$(echo "${base#*_}" | sed -E 's/^[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{4}-//')"
    cp "$f" "$out/${date}_claude-code_${slug}.md"
    echo "wrote ${date}_claude-code_${slug}.md"
  done
  shopt -u nullglob
  rm -rf "$stage"

  # Transcripts go in a repo. Read them before committing: SpecStory redacts by default,
  # but "by default" is not "verified".
  echo
  echo "Now scan for secrets before committing:"
  echo "  grep -rnE 'ghp_|github_pat_|sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}|AKIA|BEGIN .*PRIVATE KEY' $out"
}

'''
open(p,'w').write(s[:start]+new+s[end:])
print("cmd_log rewritten")
```

```bash
cd /Users/zachshort/Projects/cal.diy && python3 - <<'PY'
p='scripts/cal'; s=open(p).read()

# 1. cal log must not leave SpecStory metadata in the deliverable folder.
old="""  shopt -u nullglob
  rm -rf "$stage"
"""
new="""  shopt -u nullglob
  rm -rf "$stage"
  # SpecStory drops .project.json / statistics.json beside its output. They are tooling
  # metadata, not logs, and a dotfile is easy to miss with plain `ls`.
  rm -f "$out/.project.json" "$out/statistics.json"
"""
assert old in s; s=s.replace(old,new,1)

# 2. Stop shadowing /usr/bin/cal (the macOS calendar) for non-subcommand args.
old_shell = '''cmd_shell() {
  cat <<'EOF'
cal() {
  if [[ "$1" == "cd" ]]; then cd "$HOME/Projects/cal.diy"; else "$HOME/Projects/cal.diy/scripts/cal" "$@"; fi
}

new_shell = '''cmd_shell() {
  cat <<'EOF'
# `cal` is also macOS's calendar (/usr/bin/cal). Only take over for our own subcommands,
# so `cal 9 2026` still prints September.
cal() {
  local subs; subs=("cd" "--complete" $("$HOME/Projects/cal.diy/scripts/cal" --complete | cut -d: -f1))
  if [[ $# -eq 0 || " ${subs[*]} " == *" $1 "* ]]; then

  else
    command cal "$@"
  fi
}
'''
assert old_shell in s; s=s.replace(old_shell,new_shell,1)
open(p,'w').write(s); print("cal log + cal shell fixed")
```

## Nothing of his is in `main`

`main` has no standards or convention docs at all. Its last four commits are Oscar's and the TA's. Both of his PRs are open and **explicitly marked `WIP:`** — which, by the very rule he wrote in that doc, means "not ready to be reviewed for merging." He's drafting in the open, not inserting anything.

## And it isn't a personal doc

`docs/sprint0/standards.md` is **D3 — a required deliverable, worth 10 points**, at the exact path the spec mandates. From the Sprint 0 page: *"Each team writes an initial standards and guidelines document."* From the announcement: *"Several deliverables are shared: the standards document (D3), the sprint report (D6), and the release tag (D7) are **all one per team**."*

So there is no version of this where your team has "our own conventions" separate from his. There's one team standards document, and it's graded as a team. Asking him to keep it out of the repo would be asking him to not do an assigned deliverable — and since he's the only person who's started it, that reads poorly whatever the intent.

## What I think you actually want

Influence over what's in it. You have that already — it's a pull request, and the drafting stage is exactly when input is cheapest. Three concrete things to contribute:

1. **The empty Definition of Done.** The section exists with no content, and D3 is graded on "a coherent DoD." That's points off the whole team right now. You have a full draft ready at `docs/agent/proposed-definition-of-done.md`.
2. **The `doc:` prefix is a bug, not a preference.** `semantic-pull-requests.yml` accepts `docs:` and rejects `doc:` — following his doc literally would fail CI. Objective, easy to land.
3. **The commit style contradicts `AGENTS.md`** and the sprint spec's own example (`feat: add dark mode toggle (#17)`). D3's own rule says the project's guidelines win where they're more specific.

All three are review comments on PR #7, not a territorial conversation.

## The distinction that's actually useful

There *is* a real line between team standards and personal practice — it's the one this session has been drawing all along. Everything we built for you is **untracked and private** precisely because it's your preference and shouldn't bind anyone else. The team doc should carry only what binds everyone: the repo's conventions, the gates, the DoD.

If what's bothering you is that his draft encodes personal taste as team policy, the productive framing is *"does the project already specify this?"* — and for both conflicts, it does. That argument wins on evidence without anyone defending turf.

````bash
```markdown
# Definition of Done

an issue is done when all of these are true. where this list and the project's own
guidelines disagree, the project's guidelines win.

**code**
- [ ] the change does what the issue asked and nothing unrelated comes with it
- [ ] `yarn type-check:ci --force` passes
- [ ] `yarn lint --force` passes with no new findings
- [ ] follows the repo conventions in `AGENTS.md`: `select` not `include` in prisma queries,
      no `as any`, no barrel imports, `credential.key` never returned from an api or trpc
      endpoint, permission checks in `page.tsx` not `layout.tsx`
- [ ] any user facing string goes through `t()` and is added to
      `packages/i18n/locales/en/common.json`

**tests**
- [ ] tests written or updated for whatever changed. a bug fix should have a test that fails
      before the fix and passes after
- [ ] `TZ=UTC yarn test` passes
- [ ] tests assert behavior, not mocks

**review**
- [ ] at least one teammate reviewed it and left an actual comment, not just an approval
- [ ] the author can explain every line, including anything ai wrote

**ci**
- [ ] ci is green, and green means checks actually ran. if nothing ran, say so in the pr
      description instead of calling it passing

**process**
- [ ] branch named `feat/issue-<n>-<slug>` or `fix/issue-<n>-<slug>`
- [ ] pr description links the issue with `Closes #<n>` and explains what changed and why
- [ ] pr is under 500 lines and 10 code files, or split up
- [ ] no secrets or `.env` contents in the diff

**docs and ai logs**
- [ ] developer docs updated if the change needs it, or n/a stated explicitly
- [ ] ai session log committed to `ai-logs/sprint0/<github-username>/` and linked from the issue
- [ ] pr description says how ai was used, especially anything you changed or rejected
```

two of those need explaining because they look like nitpicks and aren't:

**why `--force` on both commands.** turbo caches both of these. i ran `yarn lint` on a clean tree and got `Tasks: 11 successful, Cached: 11 cached >>> FULL TURBO`, which means it replayed an old result and checked zero files while looking completely green. with `--force` it actually checks 3970 files. `AGENTS.md` already says to use `--force` for the type check but says nothing about lint, so lint is the easier one to get fooled by.

**why the ci line is worded weird.** looking at `.github/workflows/pr.yml`, a markdown or docs only pr runs no checks at all and the `required` job still passes, because of the paths filter. and without the `ready-for-e2e` label every build, e2e and integration job gets skipped. so "ci green" on its own doesn't always mean much and it seemed worth writing down.

also spotted two small things elsewhere in the doc that i think conflict with the project's own rules, will leave those as separate comments so this one doesn't get too long.
````

```bash
two small things i think conflict with rules the project already has. d3 says where the project's guidelines are more specific we follow the project's, so flagging rather than just having an opinion.

**the `doc:` prefix in the pull request process section would fail ci.** `.github/workflows/semantic-pull-requests.yml` runs `amannn/action-semantic-pull-request@v5` with no allowed types configured, so it falls back to the conventional commits defaults (feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, perf, test, build, ci, chore, revert). `doc` isn't in that list, `docs` is. the workflow's own failure message links to the conventional commits spec. so a pr titled `doc: whatever` gets rejected by the check. easy fix, just `docs:`.

not a big deal either way, but the first one will actually turn a check red so probably worth changing before this merges.
```
